papers.title: Host-response biomarker panels for distinguishing selected acute respiratory viral-bacterial co-infections from mono-infections.
papers.abstract: Acute respiratory viral-bacterial co-infections complicate antimicrobial decisions because pathogen detection may not establish whether both organisms are clinically contributing to disease. We synthesized evidence from adult and pediatric acute respiratory infection cohorts, including influenza, SARS-CoV-2, respiratory syncytial virus, adenovirus, and selected mixed-detection febrile illness studies, to evaluate host-response biomarkers for distinguishing co-infection from mono-infection. Conventional C-reactive protein and procalcitonin were most useful as supportive or rule-out markers of bacterial involvement, but lacked sufficient specificity when used alone. Dual-axis strategies that combine antiviral and bacterial-response signals, including MxA/CRP, TRAIL/IP-10/CRP, CD169/CD64, IFI44L/FAM89A, and targeted transcriptomic or proteomic signatures, provided more biologically coherent discrimination of mixed infection states. These findings support prospective validation of integrated host-response panels as rapid decision-support tools for antimicrobial stewardship and clinically meaningful co-infection diagnosis.

papers.title: Microenvironment shapes Staphylococcus aureus phenotypes in children with cystic fibrosis over time.
papers.abstract: Staphylococcus aureus is a common pathogen in children with cystic fibrosis (CF), frequently preceding or coexisting with Pseudomonas aeruginosa . The impact of transient P. aeruginosa infection and therapeutic intervention on S. aureus phenotypic shaping remains poorly understood. We characterized 546 isolates from a longitudinal cohort of sixteen pediatric patients in CF follow-up, either monoinfected or coinfected, over eighteen months. Isolates were grouped into three phenotypic clusters. Monoinfected patients were enriched in a cluster with high pigment and biofilm, whereas transient P. aeruginosa detection was associated with a shift toward reduced pigment and biofilm, while coinfected patients maintained stable phenotypes. Phenotypes were determined by the airway microenvironment rather than by clonal background. In two monoinfected patients, this shift coincided with transient infection and ciprofloxacin treatment with increased MRSA; in vitro , MRSA predominated over MSSA when both P. aeruginosa and ciprofloxacin were present, underscoring the need to monitor S. aureus phenotypic transitions.

papers.title: Network-based characterization of latent co-testing patterns in antimicrobial susceptibility testing.
papers.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) surveillance depends on antimicrobial susceptibility testing, yet antibiotic panels vary by pathogen cohort, specimen, year, ward, and care setting. We term these empirically reconstructed testing architectures shadow antibiograms: structures that shape which susceptibility results enter surveillance datasets and which resistance relationships can be observed. We analyzed approximately 13 million bacterial isolates from Germany's National Antibiotic Resistance Surveillance system (2019-2023) across six WHO BPPL-aligned operational cohorts. Co-testing networks were constructed using Jaccard, Dice, cosine, and phi-coefficient similarity, evaluated with Fisher's exact tests and Benjamini-Hochberg correction, and partitioned with multi-resolution Louvain community detection. Networks contained three to four dominant co-testing communities; false discovery rate (FDR) retention ranged from 89 to 100% across cohorts and specimen types. Jaccard provided the best balance of coherence, stability, antimicrobial-class alignment, interpretability, and edge retention. This work provides one of the first national-scale empirical characterizations of shadow antibiogram structure, supporting diagnostic stewardship and bias-aware AMR surveillance interpretation.

papers.title: Niche-specific immune and microbial signatures across the healthy upper respiratory tract mucosa.
papers.abstract: Host-microbe interactions in the upper respiratory tract (URT) niches that form the first line of defense against respiratory infections are incompletely understood. We profiled immune and microbial features using minimally invasive samples from 44 healthy adults (20-65 years), including nasopharyngeal (NPS), oropharyngeal (OPS), and mid-turbinate nasal swabs (MTSs), mucosal lining fluid (MLF), and saliva. Multiplex cytokine and antibody assays, 16S rRNA sequencing, and pathogen detection by PCR were performed. Immune and microbial profiles differed by niche: nasal samples showed consistently higher antiviral cytokine levels and Corynebacterium dominance. Oral samples had greater microbial diversity with distinct cytokine and antibody patterns. Saliva and MLF had the highest antibody concentrations, predominantly IgA. Integrated analyses identified site-specific microbe-immune associations. These findings show the feasibility of non-invasive, integrated profiling to uncover compartment-specific host-microbe relationships, providing a scalable framework for respiratory mucosal immunology and microbiome research with applications in infection surveillance and vaccine evaluation.

papers.title: T2T-CHM13 reference genome reduces mapping bias and enhances alignment accuracy at disease-associated variants.
papers.abstract: The T2T-CHM13v2.0 reference genome added previously uncharacterized genomic sequences and improved the accuracy of repetitive stretches compared to former human genome assemblies. By comprehensive allelic variation analysis and read mapping statistics from sequencing reads aligned to hg38 and T2T-CHM13 assemblies in samples encompassing different sequencing designs, we observed that T2T-CHM13v2.0 assembly significantly reduces the reference mapping bias (RMB) and increases read mapping precision at clinically relevant sites, including BRCA1 pathogenic variants. We report the presence of sequence dissimilarities among reference genomes in the proximity of ClinVar annotated variants, suggesting the need for data re-analysis. Analyzing DNA sequencing data from cancer patients, we identified a mean 2.3% increase in variant allelic frequency (VAF) and 0.3% increase in coverage over clinically relevant variants for samples aligned to T2T-CHM13 compared to hg38. Overall, these findings support the implementation of T2T-CHM13 reference for the improvement of sequencing data analyses in the clinical genomic setting.

papers.title: Genomic landscape of sweat gland carcinomas: Clinical applications and future directions.
papers.abstract: Sweat gland carcinomas (SGC) are rare tumors frequently driven by somatic mutations. More than 20 distinct SGC entities are recognized, many of which exhibit overlapping histopathological features, making accurate diagnosis challenging. This review provides a comprehensive overview of SGC entities and summarizes current knowledge of their mutational landscapes to improve understanding of their biology and identify potential therapeutic targets, particularly for aggressive tumors lacking treatment options in advanced stages. Key oncogenic driver mechanisms include high mutational burden, mutational signatures consistent with ultraviolet (UV)-induced DNA damage, dysregulation of the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) signaling pathway, and defects in homologous recombination-mediated DNA double-strand break repair. Recurrent, functionally significant somatic alterations have been identified in genes such as TP53, PIK3CA and CDKN2A/B, consistent with their roles in genomic stability, cell signaling and epigenetic regulation. Fusion genes represent a further key feature of SGC. Some fusion genes are entity-specific and serve as molecular hallmarks. Notably, some fusions partners have been identified in several SGC entities, suggesting shared underlying biology. Interestingly, digital papillary adenocarcinoma is the only SGC entity in which oncogenic transformation is mainly driven by a virus (HPV42). This review highlights the need for comprehensive molecular characterization of SGC and discusses the implications for prognosis, risk stratification and therapeutic decision-making. Ongoing case reporting and molecular characterization will be essential to further elucidate the molecular landscape, biological behavior, and therapeutic vulnerabilities of these rare tumors, particularly in carcinomas for which surgical excision alone is unlikely to achieve a curative outcome. Integrating broad molecular profiling with clinicopathological data and establishing systematic registries for rare cancers will be critical to advancing both biological understanding and clinical management of SGC.

papers.title: Thirty years of adjuvant therapy: From treating risk to treating residual disease.
papers.abstract: Over the past three decades, adjuvant therapy for solid tumours has evolved from treatment based predominantly on anatomical recurrence risk towards strategies informed by tumour biology, treatment response, and molecular residual disease. Cytotoxic chemotherapy and endocrine therapy established the curative potential of postoperative systemic treatment, while targeted agents and immunotherapy expanded its efficacy across malignancies. However, matching a drug to tumour biology does not establish whether residual cancer remains, and many patients receive treatment despite having been cured by surgery alone. This Perspective examines the transition from empirical risk reduction towards selective intervention against residual disease. Response-adapted perioperative strategies provide a dynamic assessment of treatment sensitivity and support postoperative escalation or omission in defined settings. Circulating tumour DNA offers a complementary approach, but its strong prognostic value must be distinguished from evidence that biomarker-directed treatment improves outcomes. Contrasting findings from randomised trials demonstrate that neither de-escalation after a negative result nor escalation after a positive result can be generalised across clinical contexts. Future studies should integrate anatomical risk, tumour genomics, pathological response, and longitudinal molecular assessment while prioritising absolute benefit, mature survival outcomes, irreversible toxicity, patient-reported outcomes, and equitable access. They should also distinguish durable eradication from temporary suppression and evaluate treatment omission with the same rigour as intensification. Progress in adjuvant oncology should ultimately be measured by additional cures achieved with less avoidable harm, through the smallest effective intervention supported by validated evidence.

papers.title: The $100 genome: three platforms reshaping clinical genomics.
papers.abstract: In 2026, three high-throughput sequencing platforms approached the widely publicised sub-$100 30× human genome. Behind these figures, which reflect consumable prices rather than total cost of ownership, the more consequential shift is the end of single-vendor dominance: these systems make comprehensive genomic profiling and multi-omic liquid biopsy feasible in small batches.

papers.title: Cerebrospinal Fluid Cytokine Signatures in Real-Time PCR-Confirmed Acute Bacterial Meningitis: Diagnostic Insights from TNF-α and IL-1β.
papers.abstract: Acute bacterial meningitis (ABM) is a rapidly progressive central nervous system infection where excessive neuroinflammation contributes significantly to morbidity and mortality. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) cytokines are key mediators of host immune responses; however, their association with molecular pathogen detection and host inflammatory responses remains incompletely understood OBJECTIVE: To evaluate CSF cytokine responses and their association with molecularly confirmed acute bacterial meningitis METHODS: A total of 246 CSF samples from patients with suspected meningitis, submitted to the department (February 2015 to January 2021) were evaluated. CSF supernatants were used for cytokine quantification, while sediments underwent bacterial culture and Real-time PCR. Cytokines (IL-1β, TNF-α, IL-12p70, IL-6 and IL-10) were measured using cytometric bead array. Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve analysis evaluated diagnostic accuracy. Bacterial DNA was detected in 53/246 (21.5%) samples, with Streptococcus pneumoniae being the predominant pathogen, particularly in children under five. Real-time PCR-confirmed cases showed significantly higher CSF TNF-α and IL-1β levels compared with non-confirmed cases (p = 0.013 and p = 0.033), indicating a predominant pro-inflammatory cytokine. Elevated IL-10 levels suggested concurrent anti-inflammatory regulation. ROC analysis demonstrated modest overall discrimination for TNF-α (AUC = 0.657, p = 0.013) and IL-1β (AUC = 0.605, p = 0.162). However, at an optimal threshold of 0.60 pg/ml, TNF-α achieved 100% specificity, establishing high reliability. Real-time PCR-confirmed acute bacterial meningitis is characterized by a distinct CSF cytokine signature reflecting coordinated pro-inflammatory activation and regulatory immune responses, highlighting CSF TNF-α as a high-specificity adjunctive to molecular assays.

papers.title: Ten simple rules to build genomics capacity for routine laboratory practice in the Global South.
papers.abstract: Developing sustainable genomics capacity in the Global South requires more than technology transfer; it depends on human-centered approaches based on the workflows and existing expertise of laboratory personnel, institutional collaboration, and long-term integration into health systems. Drawing on lessons learned from regional capacity-building initiatives, this article proposes ten simple rules for implementing and sustaining genomics capacity within public health and clinical laboratory settings. These rules emphasize local context, strategic planning, continuous learning, and equitable collaboration. Together, they provide a roadmap for laboratories aiming to transform genomic technologies from research tools for diagnosis, surveillance and decision-making, into routine instruments for public health in low- and middle-income countries.
authors: Arabela Leal E Silva de Melo

papers.title: A broad-host-range Rhizobium rhizogenes strain enables transient expression across diverse crop species.
papers.abstract: Agrobacterium-mediated transient expression has revolutionised plant research, enabling numerous landmark discoveries across diverse areas of plant biology. Yet this powerful approach remains largely confined to solanaceous species, leaving most economically important crop families without a comparable rapid assay platform. Here, we show that an engineered Rhizobium rhizogenes strain, AS109, mediates efficient transient expression across diverse dicot species spanning multiple taxonomic families, consistently outperforming commonly used laboratory agrobacterial strains. Leveraging the broad host range of AS109, we establish a suite of functional assays in faba bean (Vicia faba), including protein localisation, RNA interference-mediated gene silencing, cell-surface elicitor recognition screens, nucleotide-binding leucine-rich repeat receptor (NLR) activation, and infection cell biology at the host-pathogen interface. We further demonstrate that both singleton NLRs and sensor-helper NLR pairs from Solanaceae retain effector recognition and cell death activity when transferred into faba bean, establishing a rapid platform for evaluating cross-family transferability of disease-resistance genes. AS109 thus provides an accessible and versatile chassis for functional genomics in non-model crops, bridging the widening gap between hypothesis generation and experimental validation across diverse plant species.

papers.title: Moderate-risk variants in hereditary breast and ovarian cancer: seven-year experience from a specialized center.
papers.abstract: Moderate-risk gene variants represent an increasingly recognized component of hereditary breast and ovarian cancer (HBOC) predisposition, yet their clinical interpretation and management remain less standardized than those of high-penetrance genes. This study provides a seven-year real-world evaluation of genetic variants in ATM, BARD1, CHEK2, RAD51C, and RAD51D in individuals undergoing germline testing at a specialized HBOC center, with a particular focus on variant distribution and associated clinical management. We retrospectively analyzed germline testing data from 3416 individuals evaluated at the HBOC center Erlangen between 2018 and 2024. Testing indications included predictive as well as diagnostic and therapeutic testing in the context of breast and gynecologic neoplasms. Variant classifications followed ACMG/IARC (American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics/ International Agency for Research on Cancer) criteria. Clinical recommendations, including participation in the intensified breast cancer surveillance (IBCS) program and risk-reducing surgery, were extracted from structured counseling documentation. (Likely) Pathogenic variants in moderate-risk genes were identified across all clinical subgroups. CHEK2 represented the most frequently altered moderate-risk gene, followed by ATM. In contrast, (likely) pathogenic variants in BARD1, RAD51C, and RAD51D were observed solely among individuals undergoing predictive testing or presenting with breast malignancies. A small subset of individuals carried more than one (likely) pathogenic variant in HBOC susceptibility genes. Most women with moderate-risk variants were enrolled in the IBCS program, although in justified cases participation was withheld based on patient-specific risk factors. An isolated moderate-risk variant generally did not warrant a recommendation for risk-reducing breast surgery. Risk-reducing salpingo-oophorectomy (RRSO) was primarily discussed with individuals harboring RAD51C or RAD51D variants. Individualized modifications to the recommendations were applied especially in cases with complex genotypes comprising multiple (likely) pathogenic variants. In conclusion, this study demonstrates considerable heterogeneity in germline variants among individuals evaluated for HBOC susceptibility and highlights the particular challenges associated with interpreting moderate-risk gene alterations. The findings underscore the importance of individualized clinical assessment and support the use of real-world data to inform evidence-based surveillance and prevention strategies in hereditary cancer care.

papers.title: Developmental Systems Cardiology III: Measuring Adaptation Across the Lifespan.
papers.abstract: Developmental Systems Cardiology (DSC) conceptualizes congenital heart disease as a lifelong adaptive process shaped by interactions among biological, developmental, psychosocial, environmental, and healthcare systems. As survival has improved, contemporary challenges increasingly include neurodevelopment, psychosocial wellbeing, educational participation, healthcare engagement, and long-term adaptation, requiring multidimensional assessment beyond traditional physiological outcomes. This third article in the DSC series proposes a measurement framework for operationalizing adaptation across the lifespan. Rather than introducing new measurement domains or replacing established assessment recommendations, DSC provides an integrative architecture for linking existing measures across genomics and epigenomics, prenatal exposures, developmental physiology, neurocardiac interactions, family and social determinants, environmental influences, digital phenotyping, and healthcare-system context. Longitudinal measurement serves as a cross-cutting principle for characterizing adaptive trajectories and identifying periods of vulnerability and opportunity. Within this framework, adaptation is a dynamic, measurable process emerging through interactions among individuals, families, healthcare systems, and broader environments. Measurement therefore encompasses developmental functioning, resilience, participation, quality of life, healthcare transitions, and implementation outcomes alongside biological and clinical indicators. Established domain-specific standards, including neurodevelopmental assessment recommendations, can populate this broader architecture. This approach emphasizes integration rather than instrument development, while preserving the specificity and utility of established measures within individual domains. By integrating validated measures across domains, developmental stages, and time, DSC may provide a common language for research, registries, quality improvement, implementation science, and lifespan care. Its proposed contribution lies in organizing multidimensional measurement to better understand how adaptive and maladaptive trajectories emerge and evolve across development.

papers.title: Septic Arthritis of the Knee Caused by Neisseria meningitidis Serogroup Y.
papers.abstract: Neisseria meningitidis is a notifiable pathogen in Japan when isolated from any sterile site. We describe a rare case of primary meningococcal arthritis without meningitis or bacteremia. A 48-year-old man presented with acute septic arthritis of his knee. A synovial fluid analysis using matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization time-of-flight mass spectrometry revealed gram-negative diplococci, identified as N. meningitidis. Further antimicrobial susceptibility testing showed the isolate was pan-susceptible, allowing de-escalation from ceftriaxone to ampicillin therapy. The patient recovered fully after surgical drainage and 4 weeks of antibiotic therapy. This case highlights the importance of considering invasive meningococcal disease upon the detection of gram-negative diplococci in synovial fluid.

papers.title: Solid-state nanopore and nanochannel platforms for biomarker detection in disease diagnosis: recent advances and perspectives.
papers.abstract: Solid-state nanopore and nanochannel platforms are versatile label-free biosensors that convert biomolecular transport or binding into ionic current signals. This review organizes recent disease-diagnostic applications around a central design chain. Biomarker properties, including size, charge, conformation, abundance, and sample-matrix context, determine whether direct measurement, a molecular-recognition interface, signal amplification, or structural signal translation is required. The selected configuration then shapes the resulting signal characteristics and influences key analytical and translational parameters, including sensitivity, selectivity, dynamic range, throughput, and clinical applicability. Representative advances for protein, nucleic acid, and pathogen biomarkers in cancer, neurological disease, endocrine dysfunction, and communicable disease are critically assessed, including antibody/nanobody and aptamer interfaces, DNA nanostructures, nucleic acid amplification, electro-optical readouts, and machine-learning-assisted analysis. We further identify recurring trade-offs among analytical performance, assay time, matrix tolerance, quantitative robustness, and operational simplicity. Finally, challenges in biofouling, device reproducibility, throughput, standardization, and clinical validation are discussed together with opportunities in integrated materials, data-driven analysis, and portable systems. This framework provides practical design principles for next-generation nanopore and nanochannel diagnostic platforms.

papers.title: Ancient genomes reveal distinct human dispersals and social stratification in the settlement history of western Remote Oceania.
papers.abstract: The settlement of western Remote Oceania involved interactions among deeply divergent populations. Initial settlement ∼3,000 years ago by Lapita-associated, Southeast Asian-related groups was followed by Papuan-related expansions and later sea voyages from Polynesia. We present genome-wide data spanning the past three millennia from the eastern Solomon Islands, Vanuatu, Fiji, and Tonga. We find that the Papuan-related expansion proceeded at a slower pace than the earlier Lapita-associated expansion and reached Fiji through at least two distinct human dispersals, centuries earlier than previously suggested. We provide direct evidence of Polynesian-related gene flow at around 1,000 years ago, giving rise to Polynesian Outlier communities in southern Vanuatu. Finally, we examine an early Fijian community, revealing social practices that preserved wealth/status within a biological kin group with elevated Southeast Asian-related ancestry. Our findings refine the settlement model of western Remote Oceania and highlight the complex interplay of past migrations and community structure.

papers.title: Community-driven advances in computational mass spectrometry: The perspective of EuBIC-MS members.
papers.abstract: Advances in data acquisition, artificial intelligence, and integrative bioinformatics are driving the rapid evolution of computational mass spectrometry, and in turn, transforming modern proteomics, metabolomics, and lipidomics. These developments have greatly increased the scale and complexity of mass spectrometry data, underscoring the importance of evolving accurate, transparent, efficient and reproducible data processing workflows. Addressing these challenges requires collaborative innovation that brings together expertise in software engineering, statistics, and biology. The European Bioinformatics Community for Mass Spectrometry (EuBIC-MS), an initiative of the European Proteomics Association (EuPA), fosters a culture of open, community-driven development through its biennial Developers Meetings and Winter Schools. This commentary summarizes the scientific background and outcomes of the EuBIC-MS Developers Meeting 2025, which took place in Novacella, Italy. Three keynote presentations highlighted major frontiers in the field: deep proteome and phosphoproteome profiling, text mining for protein-protein interaction extraction, and scalable proteomics for AI-driven drug discovery. Seven community-selected hackathons addressed emerging challenges such as single-cell proteomics data analysis, FAIR metadata extraction, deep learning frameworks, R-Python interoperability, and DIA validation. Together, these efforts demonstrate the potential for scientific and technical innovation to arise from open collaboration, and highlight how community-driven initiatives can accelerate progress in computational mass spectrometry. SIGNIFICANCE: Modern proteomics increasingly depends on computational advances to translate complex, high-dimensional data into biological knowledge. The EuBIC-MS Developers Meeting 2025 exemplifies how community-driven collaboration can directly accelerate this process by bringing together experts from bioinformatics, statistics, and experimental proteomics to co-develop open, interoperable, and reproducible analytical tools. By fostering shared software frameworks, transparent benchmarking, and collaborative problem solving, the EuBIC-MS community helps ensure that technological innovation translates into reliable biological insights. This collaborative model strengthens the foundation for quantitative, system-level understanding of proteomes and establishes a sustainable path for integrating artificial intelligence and next-generation data acquisition into routine biological discovery. This commentary shows some current highlights in the field of computational mass spectrometry and community-based approaches undertaken during the most recent Developers Meeting to solve these challenges. The approaches discussed and initiated during the meeting - ranging from deep proteome profiling and phosphosite mapping to text mining, single-cell data analysis, and FAIR metadata extraction - address key bottlenecks that currently limit the biological interpretability and comparability of proteomics data.

papers.title: Cerebrospinal Fluid Transcriptional Immune Pathways Linked to Survival in HIV-Associated Tuberculous Meningitis.
papers.abstract: Tuberculous meningitis (TBM) has approximately 50% mortality in people living with HIV. We investigated differences in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) host immune responses associated with short-term mortality. We enrolled a prospective cohort of adults with HIV-related TBM in Kampala, Uganda. Metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) of bulk CSF RNA was used to detect co-infecting or alternate CNS pathogens and refine diagnoses. Host transcriptomic profiles from the refined cohort were compared between 14-day survivors and non-survivors. Cerebrospinal fluid mNGS reclassified or excluded 14% of participants based on pathogen detection, yielding 110 participants for transcriptomic analysis.Survivors upregulated T-cell receptor signaling (LCK, FYN, LAT), T-cell survival and differentiation (IL7, CD27, IL12RB1), B-cell receptor signaling (CD81, PLCG2, TNFRSF13C), cytotoxic lymphocyte and NK cell genes (KLRD1, ULBP1), TNF signaling, and class I MHC antigen processing pathways, while downregulating neutrophil chemoattractant CXCL1 and classical complement genes C4A and C4B. Unsupervised clustering identified a hypoinflammatory subgroup with significantly elevated mortality. Short-term TBM survival was associated with upregulation of adaptive immunity alongside TNF signaling and IFN-γ-driven class I MHC antigen processing pathways, with concurrent restraint of complement and neutrophil pathways. This supports investigation of adjunctive targeted agents that preserve protective responses while selectively dampening injurious innate pathways.

papers.title: CRISPR-Cas12a biosensing via transcription of crRNA from PCR or LAMP products for pathogen detection.
papers.abstract: Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats (CRISPR)-associated protein 12a (Cas12a) is an RNA-guided nuclease that has been adapted for nucleic acid-based molecular diagnostics. However, the widespread adoption of Cas12-based molecular diagnostics has been limited by dependency of a protospacer adjacent motif (PAM) sequence within the target double-stranded DNA (dsDNA) required to activate Cas12a. To eliminate PAM dependency, we explored a noncanonical activation mode by designing tailed primers for PCR to generate crRNA from amplified target dsDNA products via transcription. The transcribed crRNA, along with a dsDNA activator, then activates Cas12a. We validated this method and named it PCR followed by Transcription And CRISPR-Cas12a (PCR-TRAC). We then developed loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP)-TRAC using tailed primers. Both methods detected Mycobacterium tuberculosis genomic DNA extracted from clinical samples. LAMP-TRAC was more sensitive and faster than PCR-TRAC, detecting as little as four copies/μL of M. tuberculosis genomic DNA within 1 h. We envision that our CRISPR-Cas12-based diagnostic approach could be expanded to become a universal platform for identifying various other nucleic acid targets.

papers.title: Machine vision-integrated portable colorimetric biosensing platform with triple-layered (Pt@ZIF-8) 3 @PDA nanozymes for multiplexed ultrasensitive detection of pathogenic bacteria.
papers.abstract: Simple and in-field detection of multiple pathogenic bacteria is urgently needed. In this work, a biosensor using a nanozyme-based colorimetric immunoassay was developed for sensitive detection of multiple pathogenic bacteria. Firstly, a nanocomposite (Pt@ZIF-8) 3 @PDA-Ab was synthesized based on nanozyme coated with multiple layers of metal-organic frameworks to recognize and probe target bacteria. Additionally, leveraging the catalytic properties of Pt nanoparticles with different substrates (TMB, OPD, AEC, and ABTS), a multicolor sensor array, a portable imaging device, and an in-house coded machine vision algorithm were developed for colorimetric detecting multiple pathogenic bacteria. For single target pathogen detection, this approach exhibits a favorable linear relationship within the range of 10-10 6 CFU/mL, with a detection limit (LOD) as low as 2 CFU/mL for Salmonella Typhimurium. Furthermore, the (Pt@ZIF-8) 3 @PDA-Ab-based biosensor exhibited excellent selectivity and ambient storage stability for as long as 60 days. The colorimetric biosensing platform demonstrates excellent detection capabilities of multiple pathogens bacteria, showing a favorable linear relationship within the range of 10-10 6 CFU/mL, with LOD as low as 10, 7, 5, and 3 CFU/mL for Staphylococcus aureus, Salmonella Typhimurium, Escherichia coli, and Vibrio parahaemolyticus, respectively. The proposed sensor exhibits excellent anti-interference capability (RSD<5.8%). When applied in detecting carrot, lake water and artificial saliva samples, the method demonstrated satisfactory accuracy (RSD<5.8%) for four types of bacteria. This work highlights the synergistic integration of a structurally engineered ambient-stable nanozyme, a multicolor sensor array, and a machine vision-enabled portable device, offering a promising and generalizable strategy for point-of-need pathogen detection in food safety, environmental monitoring, and clinical diagnostics.

papers.title: Illuminating biomarkers: Metal-based strategies and fluorescence nanosensors for clinical monitoring.
papers.abstract: Plasmonic and fluorescence nanosensors have become vital tools for recent diagnostic applications due to their great sensitivity, rapid response, and capacity to determine very small amounts of biological targets. Plasmonic sensors rely on localized surface plasmon resonance (LSPR), which occurs when metallic nanostructures, such as gold or silver nanoparticles, generate strong electromagnetic fields on their surfaces. This phenomenon enables sensors to detect changes produced by biomarker or pathogen binding with great accuracy and precision. Recent advances in nanoparticle design and surface modification have improved their selectivity and appropriateness for point-of-care diagnostic devices. On the other hand, fluorescence nanosensors measure changes in fluorescence wavelength or intensity when a target analyte interacts with a fluorescent probe. Advanced fluorescent nanomaterials, including quantum dots, carbon dots, MOF-based fluorophores, and organic dyes, have significantly increased signal stability, biocompatibility, and detection limits. These developments have allowed for the sensitive determination of disease-related analytes such as nucleic acids, proteins, and metabolites. Furthermore, approaches like aggregation-induced emission and fluorescence resonance energy transfer (FRET) have improved the capabilities of fluorescence-based sensing platforms. Both plasmonic and fluorescence nanosensors provide reliable, fast, and simple diagnostic options for early illness diagnosis and clinical monitoring. This review focuses on the operating principles of both approaches, current advances in material design, and their expanding importance in diagnostic applications. This review provides a thorough resource that can successfully support and progress further research and developments in the field, particularly with regard to the applications of comparable nanosensors.

papers.title: Enzyme-Linked Cycloaddition Assay (ELCA) for Rapid, Ultra-Sensitive Monitoring of Secreted Sialoglycoproteins.
papers.abstract: Glycosylation of proteins is central to cell signaling, immune function, and pathogen interactions, yet existing methods for monitoring glycan changes require specialized instrumentation and primarily report on membrane-anchored, rather than secreted, glycoproteins. Here, we present the Enzyme-Linked Cycloaddition Assay (ELCA), a click chemistry-based platform for ultra-sensitive detection and semi-quantitative analysis of secreted sialoglycoproteins. By metabolically incorporating an azide-modified sialic acid into newly synthesized glycoproteins and capturing labeled material via strain-promoted cycloaddition, ELCA quantifies aggregate sialylation using a microplate reader-compatible, ELISA-like workflow. We demonstrate that the secreted glycoproteome responds rapidly to pharmacological perturbation, with changes detectable within hours. Benchmarking against common glycosylation inhibitors and profiling cytokine-driven macrophage polarization further establishes ELCA's sensitivity and temporal resolution. Compatible with serum-containing conditions and requiring no specialized instrumentation, ELCA provides a broadly accessible tool for rapid, cost-effective monitoring of secreted glycoprotein dynamics.

papers.title: Construction, expression, and immunogenicity analysis of a fusion gene based on the PE/PPE family in combination with adjuvants.
papers.abstract: Tuberculosis (TB) remains the leading global cause of death from a single infectious agent and a major fatal infectious disease worldwide. However, the Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccine-currently the only licensed TB vaccine in clinical practice-has critical limitations in preventing latent infection and disease reactivation, failing to deliver comprehensive protective immunity. Given these gaps, targeting Mycobacterium tuberculosis (M.tb) antigens with strong immunogenic potential is a key strategy for next-generation TB vaccine development. The pathogenic M.tb harbors the Pro-Glu (PE) and Pro-Pro-Glu (PPE) motif gene families, named for their N-terminal conserved proline (P) and glutamic acid (E) residues, which are increasingly recognized as promising vaccine targets due to their roles in host-pathogen interaction and immune modulation. To address BCG's limitations, this study selected the PE/PPE family members Rv0832 and Rv3653 for full-length gene synthesis to construct a fusion antigen designated ZMM6, which was expressed using the pET-28a vector. The immunogenicity of the ZMM6 subunit vaccine was then evaluated in M.tb-infected human cohorts and animal models. The results showed that the fusion protein ZMM6 induced peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) from M. tb-infected individuals to secrete high levels of IFN-γ, IL-2, and IL-6 cytokines. Moreover, the levels of cytokine secretion induced by the fusion protein were higher than those induced by the individual subunit proteins, suggesting that the fusion protein possesses higher immunogenicity. In mice immunized with the protein vaccine (adjuvant formulation) ZMM6/MnJ, high titers of various IgG subclass antibodies were elicited, with the immune response skewed toward a Th1-type profile, accompanied by robust induction of multiple Th1-type cytokines. Flow cytometry (FCM) analysis further revealed a significant increase in CD4 + IFN-γ + single-positive T cells in ZMM6/MnJ-immunized mice. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that the protein vaccine (adjuvant formulation) ZMM6/MnJ exhibits strong immunogenicity.

papers.title: Silicon surface multiplex immunoassay (Accuplex) for antibodies against Anaplasma spp and Ehrlichia spp is a robust option for tick-borne pathogen screening in dogs.
papers.abstract: To evaluate the diagnostic performance of a point-of-care (POC) test (SNAP 4Dx Plus; Idexx Laboratories Inc) versus a proprietary silicon surface multiplex immunoassay (SSMIA) test (Accuplex; Antech Diagnostics Inc) with indirect fluorescent antibody as the reference method (REFERENCE) for detecting antibodies against Anaplasma spp and Ehrlichia spp in dogs and to compare SSMIA test results with period prevalences reported by the Companion Animal Parasite Council (CAPC). Anonymized retention-released serum samples from dogs in the US submitted to a commercial laboratory between July 1, 2023, and September 30, 2024, were classified as true positive or true negative for each antibody via REFERENCE. Performance metrics (sensitivity, specificity, and Cohen κ) were calculated (REFERENCE as the standard) for SSMIA versus POC. Additional separate serum samples from dogs in Connecticut, Massachusetts, New Jersey, New York, and Pennsylvania underwent SSMIA testing alone in July 2024, and results were compared with respective period prevalence data reported by the CAPC. Test methods did not differ significantly for detection of antibodies against Anaplasma spp (n = 310 samples). Silicon surface multiplex immunoassay was significantly more sensitive than POC for Ehrlichia spp antibody detection (n = 309 samples). Another 2,031 samples underwent SSMIA testing alone, and positivity rates were generally higher for SSMIA detection as compared to CAPC reporting. These findings support SSMIA as a robust option for routine tick-borne pathogen exposure screening in dogs. Our work provides veterinarians with field and comparative performance data on 2 commercially available tests, informing evidence-based contextualized diagnostic options.

papers.title: MLH1 p.His112Arg Variant Is Associated With Increased Cancer Susceptibility.
papers.abstract: Lynch syndrome, a prevalent hereditary cancer predisposition, is frequently caused by pathogenic variants in the MutL homolog 1 (MLH1) mismatch repair gene. However, a significant proportion of MLH1 missense variants remain classified as variants of uncertain significance (VUS), creating clinical ambiguity. Functional validation assays in vertebrate models are crucial to assess the pathogenicity of these VUS. We previously reported the rare MLH1 NM_000249.4:c.335A>G (p.His112Arg) variant in individuals with cancer histories within the Qatar Genome Program. To assess its functional impact, we established the MLH1 p.His112Arg variant in the human colorectal cancer cell line, COLO205, using CRISPR-Cas9 technology. Isogenic wild-type (WT) and variant-carrying cells were xenotransplanted into the zebrafish. Tumor growth was quantified via fluorescence microscopy at 24 and 72 h post-injection. Zebrafish xenografted with MLH1 p.His112Arg cells exhibited a significant increase in tumor area compared to WT. This accelerated growth was associated with a significant upregulation of the proliferation marker MKI67 in variant-carrying tumors, while cyclin D1 (CCND1) and proliferating cell nuclear antigen (PCNA) (key regulators of cell cycle progression and DNA replication, respectively) expression remained unchanged, despite a tendency for increased expression. Furthermore, our functional characterization of the MLH1 p.His112Arg variant in COLO205 cells showed an enhanced proliferation capacity compared to the WT cell line, as well as increased cell viability and decreased apoptotic susceptibility when subjected to methylation-induced DNA damage. The MLH1 p.His112Arg variant confers a tumor-promoting phenotype in an in vivo zebrafish model, providing functional evidence that supports its reclassification from VUS to likely pathogenic.

papers.title: Whole-Genome Sequencing-Based Characterization and Antimicrobial Resistance Analysis of Shiga Toxin-Producing Escherichia coli Isolated from Retail Meat Products.
papers.abstract: Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli (STEC), a zoonotic foodborne pathogen, has become a critical global public health issue. This study investigates molecular traits and antimicrobial resistance (AMR) mechanisms of STEC strains derived from retail meat products sourced from domestic production in Liaocheng city, Shandong province, China, to inform health risk assessment. Using quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction (qPCR), phenotypic AMR testing, and whole-genome sequencing (WGS), 38 STEC isolates were identified from 400 retail meat products, with an isolation rate of 9.5%. Significant differences in STEC isolation rates were detected among different meat types, and mutton exhibited a relatively high isolation rate of 26.09%. Genomic virulence analysis showed that there were higher proportions of single stx 2 (58.33%) and dual stx 1 /stx 2 genotypes (33.33%) in mutton isolates than in beef ( stx 2 : 48.00%, dual stx 1 /stx 2 : 12.00%), and only the stx 2 gene was found in pork isolates. STEC isolates exhibited marked serotypic diversity, including O128ac:H2, O168:H7, O178:H7, O2:H25, and O6:H10. Multilocus sequence typing analysis revealed heterogeneous sequence type (ST) distributions among isolates, with ST10 , ST25 , and ST2722 as dominant STs, suggesting diverse contamination sources. STEC isolates exhibited high phenotypic resistance to tetracycline (TET) (68.42%), which corresponded to the highest detection rate of the TET resistance gene tet(A) at the genomic level. All isolates were susceptible to ertapenem, meropenem, ceftazidime, ceftazidime-avibactam, ciprofloxacin, and amikacin. Multidrug resistance (MDR) analysis indicated that 16 STEC isolates were MDR strains, with beef-derived isolates having relatively high MDR rates. This study verifies the occurrence of STEC in retail meat, highlighting prevalent AMR and substantial genetic heterogeneity among isolates. The findings underscore the necessity of systematic surveillance to limit STEC transmission along the meat supply chain and facilitate targeted food safety interventions.

papers.title: Green synthesis of a manganese oxide-selenium nanocomposite using watermelon peel waste with antimicrobial and mosquitocidal activities.
papers.abstract: The present study demonstrates the successful green biosynthesis of a manganese oxide-selenium nanocomposite (MnO 2 -Se NC) using watermelon peel waste extract, providing a sustainable approach for valorizing agro-industrial waste into a multifunctional nanomaterial. The biofabricated nanocomposite was characterized by UV-Vis, XRD, FTIR, DLS and TEM analysis. TEM analysis revealed predominantly spherical nanoparticles with an average size of approximately 55 nm, while UV-Vis spectra displayed two distinct absorption peaks at 266 and 300 nm, confirming successful nanocomposite formation. The MnO 2 -Se NC exhibited potent antibacterial activity, with MIC values ranging from 3.9 to 31.25 µg ml -1 and MBC values between 15.62 and 125 µg ml -1 . The highest efficacy was observed against Bacillus subtilis (MIC = 3.9 µg ml -1 ), whereas comparatively lower activity was recorded against Pseudomonas aeruginosa (MIC = 31.25 µg ml -1 ), with MBC/MIC ratios of 2-4 indicating a bactericidal mode of action. In addition, the nanocomposite demonstrated promising antifungal activity, with MIC/MFC values of 31.25/62.5 µg ml -1 against Candida albicans and 125/500 µg ml -1 against Aspergillus brasiliensis , suggesting greater effectiveness against yeast than filamentous fungi. Furthermore, the MnO 2 -Se NC showed strong larvicidal and adulticidal activity against Culex pipiens , with significantly lower LC 50 and LC 90 values (5.6-7.0 ppm) compared to the crude watermelon peel extract (66-100 ppm). These findings indicate enhanced toxicity and efficacy of the bimetallic nanocomposite at substantially lower concentrations. In conclusion, the findings highlight the considerable multifunctional potential of watermelon peel-derived MnO 2 -Se NC as a sustainable antimicrobial and vector-control agent. The combined biological activities, together with the use of an abundant agricultural waste resource for synthesis, support its future development as an environmentally friendly nanomaterial for biomedical and mosquito-management applications.

papers.title: Rapid classification of live bacteria in blood using antimicrobial peptide microarrays.
papers.abstract: The growing threat of antimicrobial resistance has made rapid and sensitive detection of bacterial pathogens in human samples an urgent need. In the case of blood infection or bacteremia, standard pathogen identification protocols are based on a two-step process. First, bacteria are cultured to increase their concentration in the sample. Then, the pathogen is assessed using cultural, molecular methods or mass spectrometry-based identification methods. To detect a larger panel of pathogens with a single, wide-spectrum microarray, we selected natural antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) and designed de novo peptides as powerful ligands for single-step bacterial classification using surface plasmon resonance imaging (SPRi). Human blood samples were spiked with low levels (less than 30 CFU ml -1 ) of clinically relevant pathogens: E. coli O157:H7 and E. coli O1:K1:H7 as Gram-negative species, as well as methicillin-resistant (MRSA) and methicillin-susceptible (MSSA) Staphylococcus aureus as Gram-positive species. One-step analysis of the samples on AMP microarrays using SPRi enabled the detection of 2.6 ± 0.2 CFU ml -1 E. coli O157:H7 in less than 10 hours and 2.7 ± 0.4 CFU ml -1 MRSA in less than 24 hours. Multidimensional analyses of SPRi data showed that a single AMP microarray can efficiently discriminate between E. coli and S. aureus strains. This process is even easier with the help of the de novo KIWI peptide. Our approach, which facilitates faster classification and identification of bacterial pathogens, paves the way for more powerful diagnostic tools in the future.

papers.title: Neuropilin-1 is involved in lytic replication in a subset of primary effusion lymphoma cell lines and for KSHV gene expression in primary endothelial cells.
papers.abstract: Primary effusion lymphoma (PEL) is a B cell lymphoma that occurs most often in people living with HIV/AIDS and is caused by Kaposi sarcoma herpesvirus (KSHV). Most are also infected with Epstein-Barr virus (EBV). While newer regimens now exist, PEL still has poorer outcomes compared to other HIV-associated lymphomas. Since PEL B cells lack typical B cell markers, we aim to identify other surface proteins in disease cells that may act as possible diagnostic or prognostic markers. We performed single cell DNA-seq and antibody derived tag-seq on BCBL1 (KSHV+/EBV-) and LCL (KSHV-/EBV+ lymphoblastoid cell line) cells to determine which surface markers are specific for KSHV+ PEL. We identified neuropilin-1 (NRP1) as a surface marker that is overexpressed in KSHV+ PEL cell lines (BCBL1, JSC1), but not in EBV+ LCL cells. NRP1 depletion during reactivation reduced lytic transcription, virion production, and infectivity of NRP1+ PEL cell lines. Selected NRP1+ PEL cells also expressed higher levels of NANOG and OCT3/4 compared to controls. NRP1+ PEL cells had higher amounts of lytic transcripts. Conversely, lytic cells express higher amounts of NRP1 transcripts at the single-cell level. Overexpression of NRP1 resulted in significantly higher lytic transcripts during lytic induction. Our findings suggest that NRP1 is a surface marker expressed for a subtype of PEL cells that is required for efficient lytic replication. It is also associated with increased expression of stemness markers, denoting poor prognosis in cancer.IMPORTANCEKSHV is a cancer-causing herpesvirus that is the etiologic agent for primary effusion lymphoma (PEL), with half of patients who are chemotherapy-resistant and have poor prognosis overall. Here, we present our discovery of NRP1 as a surface marker for a proposed subtype of PEL cell lines. We present data that support a role for NRP1 in generating infectious progeny virions and that NRP1 is associated with viral gene expression during its lytic phase. Due to NRP1's role in cancer as studied by others, it is possible that NRP1 is contributing toward worse clinical outcomes in a subgroup of people with PEL. We propose that NRP1 is a potential prognostic marker for a certain category of PEL and can be targeted in chemotherapy-resistant PEL since small molecule inhibitors against NRP1 are already available.

papers.title: Breath aerosol PCR for detection of lower respiratory tract infections: evaluation of a non-invasive face mask collector in pneumonia patients.
papers.abstract: Etiological diagnosis of lower respiratory tract infections (LRTIs) relies on sputum or bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL), which may be difficult to obtain or invasive. Exhaled breath aerosol (XBA) sampling offers a noninvasive alternative for pathogen detection. We evaluated the performance of the AveloMask, a face mask-based device designed to capture XBAs for molecular testing. In this prospective paired-sample study, hospitalized adults with pneumonia at three hospitals in Switzerland and Georgia provided an XBA sample using the AveloMask and a lower respiratory tract (LRT) specimen (sputum or BAL). XBA samples were analyzed by multiplex PCR using the Roche LightMix® panel, and LRT samples were tested using the BioFire® FilmArray® Pneumonia Panel. Concordance between XBA and LRT samples was assessed using positive percent agreement (PPA), negative percent agreement (NPA), and overall percent agreement (OPA). A total of 93 participants were enrolled, and 63 participants provided paired samples. AveloMask sampling identified the dominant pathogen (lowest Ct value in the LRT sample) in 40/47 LRT-positive cases (85.1%). Across all targets, PPA was 61% (95% CI, 50%-72%), NPA was 99.8% (95% CI, 99%-100%), and OPA was 95% (95% CI, 92%-96%). PPA was higher for bacteria than for viruses, and lower PPA was largely driven by reduced detection of low-abundance or co-infecting pathogens. In an exploratory subset analysis, AveloMask results overlapped with standard-of-care testing and may have informed antimicrobial decision-making. Breath aerosol sampling using the AveloMask enabled noninvasive molecular detection of LRT pathogens in pneumonia cases and may complement conventional standard-of-care testing, particularly when sputum is unavailable.IMPORTANCEPneumonia diagnosis often relies on sputum samples, which many patients cannot provide, or bronchoscopy, which is invasive. This study evaluated a user-friendly face mask that captures exhaled aerosols released during normal breathing and coughing for laboratory testing. In hospitalized patients with pneumonia, the mask identified the most abundant pathogen in most cases and was well tolerated in routine clinical care. These findings show that breath aerosol sampling could provide a practical, noninvasive complement to existing diagnostic methods, especially when sputum is unavailable or difficult to obtain. By making lower respiratory tract (LRT) sampling easier and more accessible, this approach could support faster, more targeted treatment decisions, reduce unnecessary antibiotic use, and expand opportunities for molecular diagnosis in hospitals and other healthcare settings.This study is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov as NCT06668883.

papers.title: Evaluation of time to antibiotic therapy after implementation of an updated rapid diagnostic test for gram-negative bacteremia.
papers.abstract: Rapid pathogen identification optimizes antibiotic therapy in bacteremia and can be achieved through molecular-based diagnostic tests. This study assesses the clinical impact after the implementation of an updated multiplex PCR panel (BIOFIRE Blood Culture Identification 2, BCID2). This single-center, retrospective, quasi-experimental study compared outcomes in adult patients with gram-negative bloodstream infections (GN-BSIs) pre and post BCID2 implementation. Data were collected from 1 March 2022 to 1 March 2024. Patients were included if they were ≥18 years of age, had a gram-negative organism identified by the panels, and received ≥48 h of antibiotics. The primary outcome was time to effective antimicrobial therapy; secondary outcomes included time to appropriate therapy, 30-day mortality, and hospital length of stay. A total of 180 patients were included (90 per BCID and BCID2 groups). Baseline characteristics were similar: median age 62 years, mostly non-critically ill, Charlson Comorbidity Index 4, and Pitt Bacteremia score 1 in both groups. Median time to effective therapy was reduced in the BCID2 vs BCID group (1 vs 4 h, P = 0.004) as well as time to appropriate therapy (25 vs 49 h, P = 0.627). In the ESBL subgroup, BCID2 significantly reduced time to effective therapy (0.5 vs 3 h, P = 0.006) and time to appropriate therapy (16 vs 44 h, P = 0.016). There was no significant difference in mortality (6.7% vs 8.9%, P = 0.756) or length of stay (10 vs 14 days, P = 0.134) between BCID and BCID2 groups. The implementation of BCID2 significantly reduced time to effective therapy in GN-BSIs, particularly among resistant organisms. This study evaluated the impact of transitioning from BCID to BCID2 panel in gram-negative bloodstream infections to address gaps in resistance detection and assess whether expanded molecular diagnostics improve time to antibiotic therapy and clinical outcomes.

papers.title: Concordance between upper and lower respiratory tract viral testing in mechanically ventilated ICU patients: A retrospective cohort study.
papers.abstract: The diagnostic value of upper respiratory tract (URT) viral testing as a surrogate for lower respiratory tract (LRT) viral detection in mechanically ventilated patients remains uncertain. We evaluated URT/LRT concordance in intubated intensive care unit (ICU) patients and identified factors associated with non-concordance. We retrospectively studied adult and pediatric ICU patients receiving invasive mechanical ventilation who underwent paired URT and LRT respiratory viral polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing between January 2014 and January 2025. Concordance was defined as detection of at least one identical virus in both specimens or negative results in both. Multivariable logistic regression identified factors associated with concordance. A simplified bedside prediction score was developed to predict non-concordance. Among 112 patients, 70 (62.5%) had concordant results. Specific positive agreement varied by virus: human metapneumovirus (88.9%), respiratory syncytial virus (80.0%), rhinovirus/enterovirus (75.0%), influenza virus (68.4%), adenovirus (34.8%), and human bocavirus (0.0%). A longer symptom-to-URT testing interval (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 0.74 per day; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.62-0.87) and chronic lung disease (aOR, 0.22; 95% CI, 0.06-0.80) were associated with lower concordance, whereas positive end-expiratory pressure > 5 cmH₂O was associated with higher concordance (aOR, 2.85; 95% CI, 1.07-7.59). The bedside score showed good discrimination for non-concordance (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, 0.818). URT/LRT concordance was moderate and varied by symptom timing, clinical factors, and viral pathogen. LRT testing may provide additional diagnostic value in patients at high risk of non-concordance. The bedside score may help identify these patients but requires further internal and external validation.

papers.title: Advanced Glycation End Products: From Pathogenesis to Treatment.
papers.abstract: Advanced glycation end products (AGEs) are chemically heterogeneous modifications generated through nonenzymatic glycation, glycoxidation, and carbonyl stress. Their accumulation increases during aging and is accelerated by hyperglycemia, oxidative stress, inflammation, exogenous exposure, and impaired renal clearance. Although AGE biology has often been framed around the AGE-RAGE-oxidative stress axis, current evidence supports a broader systems-level model in which AGE burden reflects the balance among formation, detoxification, tissue retention, and clearance. This review summarizes AGE chemistry, endogenous and exogenous sources, detoxification pathways, receptor systems, and mechanisms of AGE-mediated tissue injury. We distinguish two complementary pathogenic routes: receptor-independent structural damage, including protein dysfunction, proteostatic stress, extracellular matrix crosslinking, and altered tissue mechanics; and receptor-dependent signaling, mainly through RAGE-mediated redox-inflammatory amplification. We then examine the clinical relevance of AGEs in diabetes, cardiovascular disease, chronic kidney disease, neurovascular and retinal dysfunction, fibrosis, and aging-related tissue decline. Particular attention is given to compartment-specific biomarker interpretation, because circulating free adducts, protein-bound AGEs, tissue autofluorescence, dietary AGE estimates, and dicarbonyl stress markers are not interchangeable. Finally, we evaluate therapeutic strategies and propose a framework that matches each intervention to the relevant mechanism and can be tested clinically. In doing so, the review clarifies major conceptual and methodological uncertainties in AGE research and provides a foundation for more rigorous biomarker interpretation, study design, and clinical translation.

papers.title: Campylobacter jejuni Across the Food Chain: Integrating Pathogenesis, Persistence, Antimicrobial Resistance, and Emerging One Health Control Strategies.
papers.abstract: Campylobacter jejuni continues to be a globally important foodborne pathogen and is one of the most common bacterial causes of gastroenteritis in humans. This fastidious microaerophilic organism is seldom cultured outside of animal hosts, yet it repeatedly populates poultry, livestock, water, processing environments, retail foods, domestic kitchens, and humans. Here, we critically integrate the evidence in a transmission-connected, farm-to-fork pathway spanning colonization of animal reservoirs and carcass contamination to environmental persistence, human exposure, and disease (including antimicrobial resistance), detection, and intervention. In many systems, asymptomatic, high-density colonization of poultry is the main amplification reservoir and carcass cross-contamination, mixed-species biofilms, aerotolerance, oxidative-stress defense, cold survival, and viable-but-nonculturable cells support persistence through processing and distribution. Coordinated motility, chemotaxis, adhesion, disruption of epithelial barrier functions, invasion, and cytolethal distending toxin activity contribute to epithelial injury and inflammation, whereas lipooligosaccharide-mediated molecular mimicry contributes to postinfectious complications. Factors such as persistent target-site mutations, CmeABC efflux, acquired determinants, and antimicrobial selection within One Health compartments continue to sustain resistance to fluoroquinolones, tetracyclines, and macrolides in certain settings. Because no single point intervention can sufficiently control transmission across the food chain, effective risk reduction relies on a portfolio of components such as whole-farm biosecurity, biological control, hygienic processing and handling, cold-chain management, consumer hygiene interventions at home, antimicrobial stewardship, viability-sensitive detection and genomic surveillance. These findings are consistent with multihurdle control strategies and integrated One Health surveillance linking both animal, food, environmental, and human health sectors. Consequently, future policy and research initiatives should ideally focus on harmonized sampling and surveillance protocols, standardized outcomes of intervention studies, validation at the commercial scale and evidence directly relating C. jejuni reductions to risk of human disease.

papers.title: A Biomanufacturing Digital Twin for Consistent N-1 Seed Bioreactor Transfers for Commercial Monoclonal Antibody Production.
papers.abstract: Process consistency in biomanufacturing, particularly for commercial products, is critical for achieving consistent yield and product quality. The N-1 seed bioreactor stage, where cells grow before the transfer to a production bioreactor, often faces variability in final viable cell density (VCD), which leads to variable seeding densities in the production bioreactor and subsequent variability in total protein output per batch. In this study, we address the challenge of precise batch transfer by developing an upstream, stage-specific, level-2 digital twin (digital shadow). Here we show that a cell growth process model predicts growth accurately and updates forecasts using off-line and in-line measurements, enabling precise determination of the final sample time. Deployment of this seed transfer digital twin led to all N-1 to production transfers falling within acceptable limits and resulted in statistically significant increases in harvest yield relative to historical batches. This improvement is attributed to significantly higher on-target accuracy of final N-1 VCDs and significantly higher working volumes in the production bioreactors. Our findings demonstrate that such digital twins ensure consistent cell density during transfer, improve overall upstream process consistency, and lay a foundation for more advanced process control strategies.

papers.title: Evaluation of six generative large language models answering pre-analytical questions in medical microbiology.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have the potential to be integrated into diagnostics workflows, yet their reliability in pre-analytical diagnostic stewardship remains uncertain. We aimed to evaluate the performance of six LLMs answering common pre-analytical questions in the domain of medical microbiology. Next, we propose a blueprint to evaluate LLMs in medical microbiology. We compared general-purpose models from OpenAI (GPT-3.5, GPT-4) and Meta AI (Llama2-7B, Llama2-13B), alongside two domain-enhanced versions (customised GPT-4 agent and Llama2-7B Medical) in a hybrid evaluation framework. First, we quantified the response length (word count), then assessed the similarity between LLM-generated responses and expert-reviewed reference answers (BLEU/ROUGE scores, BERTScore). Finally, thirty-three medical professionals rated the accuracy and completeness of the LLM-generated responses on a 1-7-point scale. Responses of OpenAI models showed greater similarity to the reference set and significantly outperformed Meta AI-based models in accuracy and completeness. The customized generative pre-trained transformer (GPT) matched performance of OpenAI's general-purpose models, while generating significantly shorter responses (p<0.001). Quality ratings varied markedly between professionals, as medical microbiologists and experienced infectious disease specialists assigned significantly lower scores compared to infectious disease trainees and medical students (p<0.001). We observed considerable variation in LLM performance and highlight differences in perceived response quality across professional groups, emphasizing the need for critical appraisal when consulting LLMs for pre-analytical guidance.

papers.title: Surveillance, genetic diversity, and virulence characterisation of Francisella halioticida in blue mussels from the United Kingdom and Ireland.
papers.abstract: Francisella halioticida is a recently recognized pathogen affecting molluscs. In Europe, its presence has been documented within mussel populations in both France and England. At present, data concerning its genetic variability in mussels remain scarce. Between 2024 and 2025, a comprehensive monitoring programme was implemented to assess F. halioticida prevalence in southern England, alongside analyses of archived samples from Scotland and Ireland. The findings indicated a low prevalence of the pathogen within the surveyed populations, primarily associated with mild or localized infections. Phylogenetic analyses based on multi-locus sequence analysis showed genetic variability of F. halioticida in mussels across surveyed locations and years, however a distinct F. halioticida cluster from mussels separated from F. halioticida infecting scallops and abalone was identified. A F. halioticida metagenome assembled genome was obtained from an infected mussel from southern England, with 3666 predicted ORFs, and a ~14.2 kb region containing a putative Francisella Pathogenicity Island, including genes associated with Type VI secretion system components (TssK, DotU, IglE, and IglH), together with several hypothetical proteins, and flanked by IS3 family transposases. Additional virulence-associated genes were detected, including transcriptional and global regulators, oxidative stress and detoxification genes, and metallopeptidases. These findings improve understanding of the occurrence, diversity, and genomic features of F. halioticida in wild mussel populations, highlighting the need for expanded surveillance and higher-resolution genomic data to better understand its epidemiology and pathogenic potential. This improved resolution enhances risk assessment, enables early detection of emerging lineages, and supports more targeted monitoring strategies for wild mussel populations.

papers.title: The Emergence and Spread of Third-generation Cephalosporin-Resistant Neisseria Meningitidis in China.
papers.abstract: Neisseria meningitidis is the causative agent of invasive meningococcal disease. Although third-generation cephalosporins remain the recommended empirical therapy, there has been a growing number of globally reported isolates with resistance. This study aims to elucidate the genetic and evolutionary mechanisms underlying third-generation cephalosporin resistance in N. meningitidis. Whole-genome sequencing and phenotypic antibiotic susceptibility testing were performed, and the potential resistance determinants, genomic features, and evolutionary trajectories of resistant strains were comprehensively characterized. Seven PBP2 mutation sites potentially associated with resistance were identified, including A311V, R468K, E469K, D/N472E, L/P480A, T483S, and G545S. Genomic analysis revealed that strains possessing these seven potential resistance determinant mutations emerged within the past two decades and exhibited an increasing trend. The majority of these strains were isolated from northern regions of China. The predominant mutation strains were located in mainly epidemic strains, like cc4821, cc23, serogroup B and serogroup Y, respectively. Systematic phylogenetic analysis revealed that there has been a phenomenon of cross-regional transmission. Three potential cross-regional transmission third-generation cephalosporin-resistant strain types were identified, namely cc4821-ST-8920-NEIS1753_3923-penA795, ST-14760-NEIS1753_3652-penA1357, and cc23-ST-18108-NEIS1753_5058-penA1258. This study systematically analyzed the phenotypic and genetic characteristics of third-generation cephalosporin-resistant N. meningitidis strains. It not only deepened the understanding of the resistance mechanism but also provided a scientific basis and practical guidance for rapid clinical detection, laboratory monitoring, as well as the prevention and control of cross-regional transmission risks.

papers.title: Genomic ascertainment of systemic autoinflammatory diseases: a retrospective cohort study in two population-based biobanks.
papers.abstract: Systemic autoinflammatory diseases are rare diseases caused by innate immune dysregulation and are often linked to single-gene variants. Diagnosis remains challenging due to incomplete penetrance and variable expressivity. This study aimed to quantify the prevalence, penetrance, and clinical spectrum of systemic autoinflammatory diseases associated with pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants in 28 genes. This retrospective cohort study applied a genome-first approach to whole exome sequencing linked to electronic health records from Geisinger MyCode Community Health Initiative (USA) and the UK Biobank (UK). From a curated list of 27 dominantly inherited and one acquired disease gene, individuals with autosomal dominant pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants or somatic pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants of UBA1 were classified as cases. Variants were classified according to American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics guidelines and assigned to tier 1 or tier 2. Controls were participants without any pathogenic or likely pathogenic variant in the 28 genes. Penetrance (≥1 systemic autoinflammatory disease-associated ICD-10 code group) and clinical spectrum were assessed in tier 1 cases by comparing inflammatory ICD-10 codes and immunosuppressant use between cases and controls, with expressivity defined as the number of enriched ICD-10 code groups. Odds ratios (ORs) were calculated using Fisher's exact test with Bonferroni-Holm correction, and cohorts were analysed separately. There was no lived experience involvement in the study design or conduct. The final dataset consisted of 640 092 participants (170 503 from Geisinger MyCode and 469 589 from the UK Biobank). 280 958 (43·9%) were male and 359 134 (56·1%) were female. We identified 159 individuals carrying rare pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants in 17 genes, corresponding to a prevalence of 0·04% (63 of 170 503) in Geisinger MyCode and 0·02% (96 of 469 589) in the UK Biobank with a combined estimated prevalence of one in 4026 individuals (0·02%). Only one participant had a documented diagnosis of an autoinflammatory disorder. Geisinger MyCode cases had a disease penetrance of 79% (50 of 63) compared with a disease penetrance of 32% (31 of 96) in the UK Biobank. Overall, disease penetrance was 51%, with 81 of 159 cases exhibiting inflammatory features across multiple organ systems, especially pulmonary and cutaneous manifestations, as well as diagnoses of vasculitis (Geisinger MyCode OR 5·06 [1·01-15·54]) and rheumatic autoimmune disorders (Geisinger MyCode OR 2·29 [0·88-5·04]; UK Biobank OR 12·28 [4·12-30·68]. We also observed increased use of immunosuppressive medications in cases compared to controls (Geisinger MyCode OR 3·98 [95% CI 1·40-9·23]) consistent with clinically relevant disease. These findings suggest that monogenic autoinflammatory diseases are more common than currently recognised. Despite carrying disease-associated variants, almost no affected individuals had a documented systemic autoinflammatory disease diagnoses, pointing to a substantial gap in disease recognition and a missed opportunity to identify individuals with systemic inflammation who could benefit from genetic evaluation to guide therapy. Division of Cancer Epidemiology and Genetics, National Cancer Institute, the National Institutes of Health.

papers.title: Single-cell CRISPR screen maps epigenetic regulators of lineage specification and malignancies in human HSPCs.
papers.abstract: Mapping how genetic perturbations influence cell fate is key to understanding human development and disease. Here, we developed a massively parallel single-cell CRISPR (scCRISPR) screening platform in primary human hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs), profiling 322 regulators across 172,382 single-perturbed cells. The resulting multi-layered regulatory framework captured known associations and enabled functional annotation of regulator-phenotype relationships. Specifically, our atlas revealed that regulators acted within perturbation clusters to govern distinct gene programs that shaped cell fate. As proof of concept, we illustrated several examples. SMYD3 emerged as a negative regulator of long-term regenerative capacity. Analysis of lineage output further identified KMT5B, TRIM24, SETD7, and NSD3 as regulators associated with lineage-biased outputs. Finally, integration with clinical datasets identified PRDM10 as a candidate dependency in acute myeloid leukemia (AML). This work establishes a scalable functional genomics platform in a primary human stem cell system.

papers.title: Molecular mechanisms and regulatory networks governing Yersinia biofilm formation and host adaptation.
papers.abstract: The genus Yersinia includes three human pathogens- Y . pestis , Y. pseudotuberculosis , and Y. enterocolitica -where biofilm formation plays distinct roles in transmission and environmental persistence. All three species share the core biofilm machinery-the hmsHFRS operon, encoding enzymes for poly-β-1,6-N-acetylglucosamine (PNAG) exopolysaccharide production, and the c-di-GMP signaling controlling this production-but their regulatory networks and biofilm outputs differ. Transcriptional control of hms involves an integrated network that includes the Rcs phosphorelay (reshaped by rcsA pseudogenization), PhoP/PhoQ, EnvZ/OmpR, BarA/UvrY, Fur/Zur, CRP-cAMP, RovM/RovA, and multiple sigma factors. Post-transcriptionally, the Hfq-sRNA and CsrA-CsrB/CsrC systems modulate gene expression; the latter is directly validated in Y. pestis and Y. pseudotuberculosis , whereas its role in Y. enterocolitica is inferred from genomic conservation. At the translational and enzymatic levels, polyamines sustain Hms protein production, while redox signals govern the HmsC-HmsD disulfide switch, controlling diguanylate cyclase activity. This multi-layer architecture ensures that biofilm output is tuned to species-specific ecological niches. In host adaptation, Y. pestis transitioned from a foodborne enteric pathogen to a flea-borne lifestyle through key genetic events-acquisition of ymt , pseudogenization of rcsA , inactivation of y2909 / y3389, and ureD -which are not shared with Y. pseudotuberculosis or Y. enterocolitica , thereby explaining their different biofilm-dependent transmission strategies. Studies in Caenorhabditis elegans have identified host O-glycosylation modifications as receptors for biofilm attachment. This review summarizes progress on the molecular mechanisms, regulatory networks, and host-adaptive functions of Yersinia biofilm formation and proposes future research directions to address knowledge gaps. Future priorities include the identification of c-di-GMP effectors, flea-specific signals, 3D biofilm imaging, and CRISPR-based detection.

papers.title: Letters and Biological Process: Linguistic Structure Encodes Hierarchical Depth in the Gene Ontology.
papers.abstract: We asked whether the natural language used to name Gene Ontology (GO) Biological Process terms encodes hierarchical position in the GO directed acyclic graph. Semantic representations of term names, combined with UMAP visualization and k-means clustering (k=20) recovered biologically coherent semantic groups whose depth distributions differed strongly (Kruskal-Wallis H=5244, p<10-300; η2=0.217). Term-name length increased with depth (Pearson r=0.34, Spearman ρ=0.37; slope ≈3.2 letters per level), and this positive scaling held under shortest-, longest-, and average-path depth definitions. Vocabulary entropy followed a bell-shaped diversification-specialization curve with an intermediate-depth peak (maximal at depth 4) that lies outside a Monte Carlo null envelope across most depths, and null-model tests supported a genuine linguistic-hierarchical association. The go_lingdepth Python package, regenerated result tables, and figure-generation scripts are available at https://github.com/Sadiya-ISU/Letters-and-Biological-Process and archived on Zenodo (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.21501473). Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.

papers.title: Ketamine administered biomedically or as psychedelic-assisted therapy in treatment-resistant depression: Differing efficacy based on depressive subtype or presence of childhood trauma?
papers.abstract: ObjectiveThe ideas presented in this paper are based on a presentation at a festschrift event marking the retirement of Professor Gordon Parker from UNSW, Sydney. Drawing on Gordon's depressive subtyping approach and his critiques of a unitary view of major depressive disorder and treatment-resistant depression (TRD), we aim to (i) explore differing models of ketamine for TRD - biomedical versus 'psychedelic-assisted' therapy, and (ii) whether there may be differential efficacy in each approach based on subtype and/or childhood trauma.ConclusionPreliminary results from our study indicate in an open-label (but not randomised controlled) setting, biomedical ketamine may be superior in melancholic versus non-melancholic depression subtyped using Sydney Melancholia Prototypic Index.
