Studies of ketamine as a psychedelic agent combined with psychotherapy are lacking. We outline an empirical approach to determine whether ketamine with integrated psychotherapy has differential efficacy based on depressive subtype or past childhood trauma.

papers.title: Field Performance and usability of a novel molecular point-of-care assay for C hlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae detection.
papers.abstract: BackgroundFew studies have evaluated the field performance of novel point-of-care molecular assays for Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae . We aimed to assess the performance, feasibility and acceptability of the prototype OraSure CT/NG assay (InteliQuick, OraSure Technologies Inc., USA) among clinics in Peru.MethodsBetween May and June 2025, we recruited men and women from three clinics in Lima. Participants self-collected rectal and vaginal or penile meatal swabs and provided urine samples, while clinic staff collected pharyngeal swabs. We compared results of the prototype OraSure CT/NG assay with reference testing using the Xpert CT/NG assay (Cepheid, USA) on rectal, pharyngeal, and vaginal swabs as well as male urine, and the Aptima Combo 2 CT/NG assay (Hologic, USA) on penile meatal swabs and male urine. We applied an intention-to-diagnose framework, calculating explanatory scientific accuracy, which permits repeat testing on invalid specimens, and pragmatic application accuracy which classifies invalid results as false positives or negatives. We calculated the positive (PPA) and negative percent agreement (NPA) for each anatomic site and used closed-ended surveys to assess acceptability and feasibility among laboratory personnel.ResultsWe enrolled 157 participants. Of 470 specimens tested by the OraSure CT/NG assay, 92.3% yielded a valid result on the first attempt (99.1% after repeated testing). Among symptomatic participants, PPA for N. gonorrhoeae was 100.0% (penile meatal), 72.7% (pharyngeal), and 69.2% (rectal), while for C. trachomatis the PPA was 50.0% (penile meatal), 33.3% (pharyngeal), and 85.7% (rectal). NPA remained >90% across all sites. Seven of eight clinic laboratory personnel rated the assay as easy to use and compatible with existing clinic workflows.ConclusionsThe OraSure CT/NG assay showed consistently high NPA and was acceptable to users, while the PPA varied by pathogen and specimen type.

papers.title: A PNA-assisted magnetic bead-confined CbAgo-CRISPR/Cas12a cascade for amplification-free detection of Mycobacterium avium subsp. paratuberculosis F57 DNA.
papers.abstract: Mycobacterium avium subsp. paratuberculosis (MAP), the causative agent of Johne's disease in ruminants, has attracted increasing attention because of its potential zoonotic relevance. Sensitive molecular detection of MAP typically relies on nucleic acid amplification to overcome low pathogen abundance; however, amplification may generate nonspecific products and false-positive results. Here, targeting MAP-specific F57 double-stranded DNA, we developed a peptide nucleic acid (PNA)-assisted, magnetic bead-confined Clostridium butyricum Argonaute (CbAgo)-CRISPR/Cas12a cascade electrochemiluminescent (ECL) biosensing platform for amplification-free MAP detection. The platform comprises two functional magnetic-bead microreactors. In the PNA-CbAgo cleavage microreactor (PCCM), PNA and CbAgo/gDNA complexes are co-immobilized on magnetic beads. PNA-mediated local duplex opening facilitates CbAgo cleavage and generation of target-derived DNA fragments (tDNA). In the CRISPR/Cas12a-Ru ECL signaling microreactor (CREM), CRISPR/Cas12a-crRNA complexes and Ru-labeled ssDNA reporters are co-confined on magnetic beads. The generated tDNA activates localized CRISPR/Cas12a trans -cleavage, leading to reporter release and a target-dependent decrease in ECL intensity. Mechanistic studies showed that the PCCM enhances tDNA generation through PNA-assisted duplex opening and bead interfacial confinement, whereas the CREM enables efficient ECL transduction through localized CRISPR/Cas12a-crRNA-reporter coupling. Under optimized conditions, the platform achieved a detection limit of 34.1 CFU mL -1 , exhibited good specificity, agreed well with qPCR in spiked bovine fecal samples, and demonstrated robust overall performance in complex matrices. This work provides an amplification-free ECL strategy for sensitive and specific MAP detection and highlights the potential of bead-confined programmable nuclease cascades for pathogen nucleic acid analysis.

papers.title: PgaR is a positive regulator of the pgaABCD biosynthetic operon in Klebsiella pneumoniae.
papers.abstract: The biosynthetic locus encoding the exopolysaccharide poly-N-acetyl-glucosamine (PNAG) is widely conserved across bacteria, including the World Health Organization critical-priority pathogen Klebsiella pneumoniae (Kp). In Kp, PNAG synthesis is mediated by the pgaABCD operon, yet its lineage-specific regulation remains incompletely understood. Using a comparative genomics approach to interrogate the pgaABCD locus across the high-risk clonal Kp complex 258 (CC258) lineage, we identified a previously uncharacterized positive transcriptional regulator located immediately upstream of pgaA , which we designate pgaR . Phylogenetic analysis revealed recurrent evolutionary events affecting this regulatory region, including repeated deletion or truncation of pgaR and a G > A substitution upstream of the pgaR start codon. Functional characterization demonstrated that loss of pgaR abolishes pgaABCD expression and PNAG production, whereas the upstream G > A substitution drives PNAG hyperproduction. Under in vitro growth conditions, Kp produce extensive extracellular PNAG networks. Using a prototype hypervirulent strain to model the role of PNAG in vivo indicated that it is dispensable for virulence in murine pneumonia and peritonitis models. In contrast, PNAG hyper-production significantly attenuated virulence and reduced disease severity. Collectively, these findings identify PgaR as a novel upstream gene regulator of the pgaABCD operon and reveal a previously unrecognized lineage-specific layer of PNAG regulation in Kp. This demonstrates that opposing PNAG phenotypes, loss and hyper-production, have independently and repeatedly emerged among clinical CC258 isolates, highlighting selective pressures acting on this locus.

papers.title: Host- and pathogen-regulated exocytosis facilitates dynamic distribution of endolysosomal content during infection by the vacuolar pathogen Coxiella burnetii .
papers.abstract: Coxiella burnetii is an obligate intracellular bacterial pathogen that causes the zoonotic disease Q fever. Coxiella extensively subverts host vesicle traffic and replicates within lysosome-derived, spacious vacuoles by secreting a suite of effectors through the type IVB secretion system (T4BSS). This study investigates the regulation and role of a fundamental lysosomal process, exocytosis, in the prolonged maintenance of Coxiella vacuolar niche. Biochemical, microscopic, and proteomic approaches indicate that infection promotes release of extracellular vesicles (EVs). Increase in extracellular levels of endolysosomal proteins and surface localization of LAMP1 were identified in both phagocytic and non-phagocytic cells, during later stages of infection. Interestingly, infection-induced exocytosis was dependent on the activity of the bacterial T4BSS. On one hand, knockdown of the lysosomal master transcriptional regulator TFEB significantly reduces basal exocytosis and enhances intracellular Coxiella replication, while deficiency of the exocytosis-associated SNARE, Syntaxin 11, does not reduce basal exocytosis and yet, increases Coxiella replication, suggesting that host exocytosis is not the sole or a dominant determinant of the infection process. On the other hand, modulating the activity of a key host exocytosis regulator- the calcium channel TRPML1, decreases intracellular Coxiella replication suggesting a tightly regulated role of TRPML1. Infection was also associated with the extracellular detection of LAMP1-associated Coxiella , suggesting an encased egress mechanism. Together, this study demonstrates that Coxiella infection activates exocytosis in a temporal, host-, and bacterial factor-dependent manner.

papers.title: A plasmid-encoded T3SS underlies the virulence of enteropathogenic Providencia alcalifaciens strains isolated from a large foodborne outbreak in Japan.
papers.abstract: Providencia alcalifaciens is a gut commensal bacterium and also an emerging enteric pathogen associated with sporadic infections and outbreak cases in humans. The most notable outbreak caused by this bacterium occurred in 1996 in Fukui Prefecture, Japan, affecting 270 individuals. However, the pathogenic mechanisms responsible for this outbreak remain unknown. In this study, we identified the key virulence determinants of the Fukui outbreak strains through genomic and functional analyses. These strains uniquely carry a ~162 kb large plasmid encoding a type III secretion system (T3SS) closely homologous to the Salmonella SPI-1 T3SS. We also show that the plasmid-encoded T3SS (T3SSp) constitutes a functional secretion system and is essential for the pathogenicity of the Fukui outbreak strain, including the invasion of cultured epithelial cells and the induction of diarrhea in a rabbit model. Secretome analysis identified effectors secreted in a T3SSp-dependent manner, among which PipA-sharing limited sequence similarity with SipA, a SPI-1 T3SS effector-plays a crucial role in inducing diarrhea. Ectopic expression of PipA in HeLa cells caused focal accumulation of F-actin, indicating its cytoskeleton-modulating activity. Comparative genomics with other Providencia species revealed the dissemination of the large plasmid, with structural variations among enteropathogenic strains of P. alcalifaciens and Providencia rustigianii associated with clinical cases in humans and animals. Thus, our findings underscore the molecular basis of P. alcalifaciens pathogenicity in the Fukui outbreak and highlight the significance of the large plasmids encoding T3SS in driving pathogenic evolution among Providencia species.

papers.title: Multiplex digital PCR for rapid quantitative detection and dynamic monitoring of respiratory pathogens in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid.
papers.abstract: Lower respiratory tract infections (LRTIs) remain a leading cause of mortality worldwide. Rapid and comprehensive etiological diagnosis is critical yet challenging: existing approaches, from culture to multiplex PCR and mNGS, carry distinct limitations in one or more of turnaround time, sensitivity, cost, or quantitative resolution. We developed a 33-plex digital PCR (dPCR) assay for absolute quantification of bacteria, viruses, fungi, and atypical pathogens in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF). Systematic evaluation of five liquefaction protocols identified dithiothreitol (DTT) as the optimal universal pretreatment, ensuring balanced RNA and DNA recovery. The assay demonstrated reliable quantification from 10 to 10 5 copies per test for all 33 targets ( R 2 > 0.99), with 27 targets showing linearity across full range and 6 targets exhibiting linearity from 10 to 10 4 copies per test (10 5 as upper detection limit). The limit of detection was 5 copies per test for all targets. In 105 BALF samples, dPCR achieved a significantly higher positive rate than culture (96.19% vs. 83.81%, p < 0.05), particularly for polymicrobial infections (85.71% vs. 40.00%). Concordance with mNGS for primary pathogens was 86.96% (20/23) for 14 primary pathogens across 23 positive samples. The complete workflow from sample pre-treatment to results required only 2.5 hours. Serial BALF dPCR quantification of P. aeruginosa and K. pneumoniae in one severe LRTI case tracked pathogen loads in parallel with clinical course and antibiotic responses, preliminarily supporting the technical feasibility of dynamic monitoring. This study demonstrates the feasibility of a rapid 33-plex dPCR assay for comprehensive respiratory pathogen profiling in BALF, with potential for dynamic monitoring in critically ill patients.

papers.title: Do LLM Proposers Improve Budgeted Search for Ionizable Lipids?
papers.abstract: Efficient lipid design under limited experimental budgets is a central challenge in computational chemistry and drug discovery. We introduce LEAF (Lipid Evolutionary Adaptive Framework), a matched-budget protocol for testing whether language-model proposers improve combinatorial molecular search relative to classical baselines. The study uses a 30,044-candidate ionizable-lipid space, a frozen Gaussian-process oracle fitted to experimental potency labels, and a separate active-learning surrogate. Four language models evaluated over eight seeds and three splits show no significant improvement over genetic-algorithm or random-search baselines. For Llama 8B, 79.1% of acquisition-selected queries repeat previously evaluated archive members. Removing duplicates reduces the performance gap on some splits but increases proposal cost and can prevent budget exhaustion. Larger models reduce duplication without establishing superiority or equivalence. Exploratory scored prompts and stricter novelty controls yield positive median differences against the genetic algorithm, yet wide intervals and shared-seed dependence preclude stronger conclusions. A validated single-assay reanalysis preserves the chemotype-cold deficit at a smaller numerical scale, and exploratory expected hypervolume improvement does not reverse the result. Follow-up checks address whether proposers genuinely use injected evidence. These checks include a zero-shot leakage probe, rank-only and chain-of-thought-rationale prompts, a score-shuffle perturbation, an evidence-conflict probe, and a genuine reasoning-mode proposer. They show measurable engagement with supplied information without a corresponding performance gain. LEAF isolates proposal quality as the experimental variable and documents a concrete failure mode of zero-shot LLM proposers under controlled budgets.

papers.title: BioMod: Biological Module Tokenization for Single-Cell Foundation Modeling
papers.abstract: Single-cell foundation models typically represent cells as flat sequences of individual genes, requiring higher-order biological organization to be inferred implicitly from sparse expression profiles. Similar to the evolution from character-level to semantic tokenization in natural language processing,we hypothesize that cellular states can be more efficiently represented using biologically meaningful intermediate units. Here we present BioMod, a 50-million-parameter single-cell foundation model that introduces biological modules as representation units between genes and cells. BioMod constructs an overlapping vocabulary of 660 biological modules derived from curated pathways and data-driven gene programs, replacing thousands of gene-level inputs with compact module representations. Pretrained on approximately 73 million human cells using high-ratio module masking with an asymmetric decoder, BioMod achieves state-of-the-art performance across cell-type annotation, zero-shot batch integration, perturbation-response prediction and drug-response forecasting while maintaining a compact architecture that enables efficient inference on a single GPU. Module-level analyses further demonstrate that BioMod captures biologically meaningful cellular programs and preserves pathway-level organization.

papers.title: Progranulin deficiency promotes neuroinflammation through cathepsin B-mediated activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome
papers.abstract: Haploinsufficiency of progranulin (resulting from mutations in the GRN gene) is a major genetic cause of frontotemporal dementia (FTD), which is characterized by profound changes in personality and behavior, progressive impairments in executive function, speech, language and/or movement, TDP-43 pathology, lysosomal dysfunction, and neuroinflammation. Studies in progranulin-deficient mouse models have demonstrated the critical role of neuroinflammation in disease pathogenesis, as deletion of NF-kB or complement factors prevents FTD-associated behavioral deficits. While progranulin is known to be anti-inflammatory, the precise molecular mechanism by which its deficiency triggers inflammatory cascades remain unclear. Here, we investigate the involvement of the NLRP3 inflammasome in progranulin-deficient models, including mice, human microglial cells, and patient fibroblasts. In Grn mice, we found increased levels of several inflammasome-related proteins, including procaspase-1 and cleaved IL-1{beta}. Similarly, GRN knockout (KO) microglia cells showed significant increases in levels of procaspase-1, NLRP3, and cleaved IL-1{beta}. Moreover, KO cells had increased NLRP3 oligomerization, suggesting that progranulin negatively regulates inflammasome assembly. We also investigated the potential link between lysosomal dysfunction and NLRP3 inflammasome activation in progranulin deficiency. We found that pharmacological inhibition of cathepsin B reduced NLRP3 inflammasome oligomerization as well as inflammatory cytokine expression in GRN KO cells. Additionally, siRNA knockdown of cathepsin B reduced levels of procaspase-1 and cleaved IL-1{beta} in GRN KO cells. Finally, we found that heterozygous GRN fibroblasts exhibited similar increases in procaspase-1 and cleaved IL-1{beta} levels, and these increases were corrected by treatment with an antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) that increase progranulin protein levels. Overall, our results demonstrate that progranulin deficiency promotes NLRP3 inflammasome assembly and activity through cathepsin B-mediated signaling, thereby establishing a mechanistic link between lysosomal dysfunction and increased inflammation. The ability of the GRN-targeting ASO to correct NLRP3-mediated inflammation highlights a promising therapeutic strategy for FTD-GRN and inflammation in other neurodegenerative disorders linked to progranulin deficiency.

papers.title: Spatially resolved tumor-microenvironment architecture defines therapeutic response in unresectable hepatoblastoma
papers.abstract: Background: Hepatoblastoma exhibits variable therapeutic response that is not fully explained by current risk stratification. While prior studies have characterized tumor composition, the role of spatial organization in determining outcome, particularly in unresectable disease requiring transplantation under immunosuppression, remains unclear. Methods: We integrated spatial transcriptomics using the 10x Genomics Visium platform (n = 11 tumors) with single-cell spatial molecular imaging using NanoString CosMx (n = 3 tumors) on post-chemotherapy explant specimens across clinically defined groups (relapse-prone unresectable, non-relapse unresectable, and resectable hepatoblastoma). Spatial deconvolution, module scoring, spatial co-localization, and cell-cell interaction analyses were used to define region-level transcriptional programs and their underlying cellular organization. Results: We identified three spatial architectures associated with clinical outcome. Relapse-prone tumors exhibited a centralized, TME-dominated organization enriched for progenitor-like, cycling, and stress-responsive tumor cell states co-localized with SPP1+ TAMs and CAFs, with enrichment of hypoxia response, extracellular matrix remodeling, and Midkine (MDK-LRP1) signaling. Non-relapse tumors displayed a distributed architecture with compartmentalized tumor-immune interactions, increased immune engagement, and preserved epithelial differentiation, including inflammatory hepatocyte-like states. Resection samples showed reduced tumor cell state heterogeneity and more uniform TME-immune organization. Conclusions: Integration of regional and single-cell spatial transcriptomics across two platforms reveals that the chemo-remodeled tumor architecture of hepatoblastoma encodes spatially organized tumor cell-TME interactions as central determinants of therapeutic response.

papers.title: Human caspase-4 and caspase-5 assemble into non-canonical inflammasomes in response to overlapping and distinct LPS structures
papers.abstract: Innate immune sensing of bacterial lipopolysaccharide (LPS) is critical to host defense, but a dysregulated response can lead to sepsis, a life-threatening condition associated with multiple organ failure and shock. LPS is sensed at the cell surface by Toll-Like Receptor 4 (TLR4) and in the cytosol by mouse caspase-11 (Casp11) or its human orthologs, caspase-4 and 5 (CASP4/5). In response to cytosolic LPS, Casp11 oligomerizes in a catalytically dependent manner into supramolecular organizing centers (SMOCs). We demonstrate that CASP4 and CASP5 also form catalytically dependent SMOCs in response to bacterial LPS in macrophages. Furthermore, we find that CASP4 and CASP5 differentially respond to distinct LPS structural variants that fail to activate CASP11 and that only activating LPS structures induce SMOC formation by the corresponding caspase. Notably, transgenic mice expressing CASP4 in lieu of Casp11 exert more effective control of Francisella novicida, a rodent pathogen whose LPS evades TLR4 and Casp11 detection. Conversely, CASP4-expressing mice are more susceptible to sepsis when exposed to E. coli expressing a lipid A variant that fails to activate TLR4 and Casp11. Together, these findings reveal human CASP4 and CASP5 have evolved to assemble into SMOCs in response to a broader range of LPS structures than mouse Casp11 and highlight the potential tradeoff between systemic inflammation and control of bacterial infection that may underline these differences. Our findings may inform the development of targeted therapeutic strategies for gram-negative bacterial infection and sepsis that are effective in humans.

papers.title: VirtualSkin integrates skin-cell identity with intervention-response prediction
papers.abstract: Human skin atlases resolve a diverse set of cellular states, yet connecting these states to their responses to intervention remains difficult across independently sampled tissues. Here we present VirtualSkin, a cell language model that aligns skin transcriptomes with biological descriptions and supports intervention conditioned response prediction. We evaluated the model across independent atlas, disease, anatomical and perturbation cohorts, with donors, studies and perturbations withheld according to the experimental design. VirtualSkin improved inflammatory skin annotation by 0.056 macro F1 points and cell text retrieval by 0.12 Recall@10 points relative to the strongest corresponding comparators. The representation retained cell identity during study integration and transferred across ageing, systemic sclerosis, lymphoma and anatomical sites. Across five intervention cohorts, response prediction improved by 0.03 0.09 response-score points, with agreement at the levels of gene expression change, gene recovery and transcriptional programs. Paired tissue trajectories provided a complementary assessment in two donors per intervention. Component ablations and pairing controls localized the predictive contributions, while uncertainty estimates supported selective prediction under distribution shift. These results connect skin-cell recognition to intervention response prediction within a common evaluation framework and define the conditions under which predictions can inform experimental prioritization.

papers.title: Towards Robust Automated Mouse Scratching Behavior Detection for Itch Research
papers.abstract: Automated detection of mouse scratching behavior could reduce manual annotation and is essential for preclinical itch research. However, robust performance across laboratories remains a challenge for current methods. We present Scratch-AID+, a framework dedicated to automated mouse scratching detection, including a diverse and progressive set of approaches: classic ResNet-based detectors, task-adaptive fine-tuning of video foundation models, and in-context learning with advanced multimodal large language models. To simulate real-world use cases, we benchmark on a public dataset and utilize additional cross-laboratory video recordings for independent testing. We find that classic baselines suffered severe performance degradation on external data under the realistic setting with sparse scratching events. In contrast, fine-tuned video foundation models successfully bridged this generalizability gap, achieving significantly better detection performance. Furthermore, frozen multimodal large language models demonstrated promising out-of-the-box ability using only few-shot demonstrations. We also examined the effects of different video preprocessing strategies. Our findings highlight the improved performance and generalizability of the adapted foundation models for automated scratching behavior analysis and shed light on the real-world deployment of such detectors. Our code is publicly available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/scratch aid-plus/.

papers.title: Decoding super-enhancer regulatory grammar and pathogenic gain-of-function variants directly from DNA sequence
papers.abstract: Super-enhancers (SEs) drive cell-identity gene expression, yet their identification relies on epigenomic profiling (e.g., H3K27ac ChIP-seq), precluding discovery in unprofiled cellular states and leaving their underlying sequence grammar unknown. Here, we present Borzoi-SE, a deep learning framework built upon the genomic transformer Borzoi that formulates SE discovery as hierarchical, cell-type-resolved genomic object detection directly from long-range sequence across 90 human lineages. Base-resolution attribution recovers lineage-defining master transcription factors across cell types. Within SEs shared across lineages, it reveals lineage-dependent motif usage, suggesting that the same regulatory regions can support distinct cell-type-specific programs. Using in silico ablation, Borzoi-SE decoded the functional hierarchy of the {beta}-globin super-enhancer, prioritizing hypersensitive site 2 (HS2) as the dominant constituent, which we experimentally verified via CRISPR interference. Trained without variant-effect labels, Borzoi-SE identified gain-of-super-enhancer variants in different tissues. At the CHRM2 locus, a single-nucleotide variant created a de novo glucocorticoid receptor (GR) motif that recruited activated GR and potentiated adjacent MEF2 regulatory syntax, nucleating a cardiac super-enhancer. Orthogonal multi-omics and population-genetic evidence linked this variant to increased CHRM2 expression and variation in resting heart rate and PR-interval duration. Borzoi-SE establishes a general framework for decoding SE regulatory grammar and prioritizing causal non-coding variants directly from sequence.

papers.title: A multimodal precision oncology platform integrating genomics,single-cell transcriptomics, and functional drug screening expandstherapeutic options in pediatric brain tumors
papers.abstract: Precision oncology for pediatric brain tumors mainly relies on clinically validated, targetable genomic alterations, which are often sparse, yield few matched therapies, and do not guide chemotherapy selection. We developed a tiered framework in which deep whole-genome sequencing and single-cell RNA sequencing extend targeted-therapy selection, with ex vivo functional drug screening supporting selection of both targeted therapies and chemotherapies. We applied it to 17 children with malignant CNS tumors. The approach expanded recommendations beyond genomics: functional screening provided every patient with at least one high-confidence targeted-therapy or chemotherapy nomination, while single-cell RNA sequencing identified an average of 37 druggable gene targets per patient, producing a fourfold increase in high-confidence targeted-therapy recommendations. In an exploratory analysis, functional classifications were directionally consistent with outcomes in 8 of 10 evaluable cases, although combination treatments and radiation precluded causal attribution. Single-cell profiling also identified subclone-specific vulnerabilities, supporting prospective evaluation of the platform's feasibility and predictive utility.

papers.title: Predicting resistance to synthetic lethal therapies in cancer
papers.abstract: Background Synthetic lethality (SL) occurs when an alteration in one gene renders cells vulnerable to inhibition of another, offering a strategy for targeted cancer therapy. PARP inhibitors represent the first clinically approved synthetic lethal therapy, and numerous additional candidates are now in clinical trials. Unfortunately, resistance to these therapies is common and impairs their overall effectiveness. Although there is a growing understanding of the factors that predict synthetic lethal interactions, the prediction of mechanisms driving resistance to these effects remains largely unstudied. Here, we sought to determine whether SL resistance could be predicted a priori using protein-protein interaction networks integrated with additional molecular profiles. Methods We curated genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 chemogenetic resistance screens spanning ten unique SL biomarker-target pairs. For each pair, we extracted resistance genes and computed features capturing protein-protein interactions, gene expression, and essentiality. We compared these features between resistance and non-resistance genes and developed a random forest classifier to predict resistance. Model performance was assessed using random-split and structured leave-one-out schemes based on biomarkers, targets, and SL pairs to ensure robust generalisation. Independent validation of the model was performed by assessing its ability to predict resistance to two SL therapies currently in clinical trials, MTAP-PRMT5 and ATM-ATR. Results Resistance genes were significantly enriched among the protein-protein interaction partners of SL pairs across multiple datasets, suggesting functional interaction networks can aid the prioritisation of resistance mechanisms. Resistance genes tended to be more co-expressed with their associated target and also displayed distinct essentiality patterns. Although no individual feature was strongly predictive, integrating all features in a random forest model improved discrimination between resistance and non-resistance genes. Under leave-one-SL-pair-out cross-validation - our most stringent test of generalisation - the model achieved a mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.72 across ten pairs (range 0.57-0.91; mean average precision ~9%); a random train-test split gave a higher AUROC (~0.78) that we treat as an optimistic upper bound, since biomarkers and targets are shared across folds. Average precision remained low in absolute terms, reflecting the inherent challenge of predicting extremely rare resistance events (<1% of genes). Conclusions Resistance to synthetic lethal therapies arises, at least in part, from predictable patterns of network connectivity, transcriptional coordination, and context-dependent essentiality. Our integrative framework provides a computational approach for anticipating resistance mechanisms across the expanding landscape of synthetic lethal therapies, offering a foundation for designing more durable and effective combination treatments.

papers.title: PlantGeneAnn: a high-accuracy ab initio plant gene annotation tool fine-tuned from a genome foundation model
papers.abstract: Structural annotation remains a bottleneck for translating the growing catalog of high-quality plant genomes into biological insights, as current pipelines rely on RNA-seq and homologous protein evidence that are often unavailable for non-model species. Existing ab initio tools are constrained by model scale and perform poorly in complex plant genomic regions. We present PlantGeneAnn, a plant-optimized ab initio gene annotation tool fine-tuned from a genome foundation model. It combines a Mamba-MoE DNA encoder with a U-Net-style embedding decoder and a semi-Markov decoding pipeline. Trained on 40 angiosperm species, PlantGeneAnn establishes a new state-of-the-art (SOTA) across a stringent 20-species benchmark, significantly outperforming Helixer, Tiberius, and ANNEVO at exon-, intron-, and locus-levels, with mean F1 scores of 0.856, 0.880, and 0.707, respectively. It also enables efficient customized fine-tuning: LoRA fine-tuning increased the locus-level F1 of the out-of-distribution bryophyte Physcomitrium patens from 0.581 to 0.736, with performance plateauing at 40% of the fine-tuning data. Notably, PlantGeneAnn requires substantially lower peak memory usage than other baseline tools, allowing annotation of large plant genomes on standard personal workstations. PlantGeneAnn thus provides accurate, hardware-friendly ab initio annotation for diverse plant genomes, particularly newly assembled genomes, population-scale projects, and non-model plants.

papers.title: Language eligibility criteria and enrolled racial and ethnic composition in US clinical trials: a cross-sectional study
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Federal policy now requires sponsors to submit diversity action plans for clinical trials, yet the modifiable features of trial design associated with enrolled composition remain poorly characterized. English-language proficiency requirements are written into eligibility criteria and recorded as free text in a public registry, making them visible and, in principle, amenable to revision, but their relationship to enrolled composition has been examined only within single disease areas and in small samples of trials. We examined whether these requirements and documented language accommodation were associated with the racial and ethnic composition of enrolled participants. METHODS AND FINDINGS: We conducted a cross-sectional study of interventional trials registered on ClinicalTrials.gov with at least one US site and posted results, using a registry snapshot retrieved in October 2026. The primary cohort comprised the 44,487 trials with exclusively US sites, of which 21,924 (49.3%) reported baseline race and 17,434 (39.2%) reported baseline ethnicity with counts that reconciled with the posted denominator. Both exposures were classified from free-text eligibility criteria using regular expressions validated against independent physician review of 150 trials. For the English-language requirement classifier, sensitivity was 88.2% and specificity was 99.2%. The outcome was the trial-level proportion of enrolled participants in each category, analyzed using generalized linear models adjusted for intervention class, therapeutic area, sponsor, phase, enrollment, sites, start year, US Census region, and the population composition of the trial's site states. An English-language proficiency requirement appeared in 5,736 trials (12.9%); its prevalence rose from 7.4% of trials starting in 2010 to 26.2% in 2023 (odds ratio [OR] per decade 2.91, P<0.001), whereas documented accommodation, an eligibility statement allowing participation in a language other than English (Spanish in 99.9% of flagged trials), remained rare (788 trials, 1.8%). The requirement was associated with lower enrolled proportions of Asian (OR=0.85, 95% CI 0.77-0.93, P=0.001) and Hispanic/Latinx participants (OR=0.85, 95% CI 0.79-0.91, P<0.001), with no evidence of an association for White participants (OR=0.99, 95% CI 0.95-1.04, P=0.75). Documented accommodation was associated with a higher proportion of Hispanic/Latinx participants (OR=3.23, 95% CI 2.82-3.71, P<0.001). Geographic adjustment did not change the statistical significance of the requirement associations and attenuated the accommodation association. The main limitations were the cross-sectional design, which precludes causal inference; the restriction of enrollment analyses to trials reporting baseline demographics, which were more recent than those without such reporting; and possible misclassification of automatically classified exposures. CONCLUSIONS: English-language proficiency requirements became more than three times as common between 2010 and 2023 and were associated with lower enrolled proportions of Asian and Hispanic/Latinx participants. Less common documented language accommodation was associated with a higher enrolled proportion of Hispanic/Latinx participants. Because these criteria are investigator-written and publicly recorded, they may be a tractable target for improving enrollment equity, although whether revising them changes who enrolls requires prospective evaluation

papers.title: Long-read sequencing and benchmarking of saliva against blood for genomic variant detection in autism
papers.abstract: Autism is highly heritable, yet many cases remain genetically unsolved even after short-read sequencing (SRS). Long-read sequencing (LRS) increases sensitivity for pathogenic variant discovery, especially for complex structural variants (SVs) in repetitive regions missed by SRS. However, LRS largely relies on blood-derived DNA; whether saliva can support genome-wide LRS at population scale remains to be seen. We report the first systematic evaluation of saliva-derived DNA for genome-wide LRS in autism, benchmarking 105 new saliva samples against 68 new blood samples and integrating 189 previously published LRS blood samples to expand the autism cohort and improve ultra-rare pathogenic variant discovery. A matched blood-saliva quad provided direct comparisons of variant detection between sample sources. Saliva samples contained substantially more nonhuman DNA than blood (mean 10% versus 0.005% of reads), reducing mean effective genome coverage from an estimated 28X to 24X after removal of nonhuman reads, compared with 34X in blood samples. Despite this reduction, saliva and blood samples yielded comparable numbers of validated (22,591 versus 23,064) and rare (209 versus 213) SVs per sample, which was also observed in the quad when matching coverage. Saliva LRS identified four new pathogenic and likely pathogenic variants missed by SRS. We report variants affecting MECP2, DNMT3A, CHD8, LMBRD2, POGZ, and PHF3; four additional candidates with potential relevance to autism; and an increase of diagnostic yield of 9-18%. Saliva-derived DNA support blood-comparable discovery of pathogenic variants missed by SRS, including SVs, with increased sequencing coverage compensating for nonhuman DNA contamination and reduced assembly contiguity, thus showing saliva DNA collection as a feasible strategy for large-scale LRS studies of patients and population-scale sequencing of cohorts.

papers.title: A national ecosystem for long-read genome sequencing: Integrating population genomics and rare disease diagnostics in Sweden
papers.abstract: To evaluate the clinical implementation of long-read genome sequencing (lrGS) and establish the population reference resources needed to support its use in diagnostics, we integrate two complementary initiatives: Genome of Sweden (GoS), Sweden's contribution to Genome of Europe (GoE), and the Genomic Medicine Sweden - Rare Diseases (GMS-RD) long-read sequencing pilot. The initial GoS release of 576 individuals provides population-scale maps of genetic and epigenetic variation. Among 485 GMS-RD probands, 161 (33.2%) receive a molecular diagnosis, with lrGS providing added clinical value in 40 (24.8%). As a first-line test, lrGS could have avoided at least 42 follow-up analyses and an additional testing cycle in 7.2% of probands, reducing costs and the burden on patients. By integrating population and clinical long-read genomics, Sweden establishes a national ecosystem for genomic research and clinical diagnostics. Our findings support the clinical implementation of lrGS and offer a scalable model for national collaboration.

papers.title: Enhancing molecular and genomic approaches for Bordetella pertussis investigation and public health surveillance in Victoria, Australia
papers.abstract: Bordetella pertussis is the main aetiological agent of pertussis (whooping cough), with a global resurgence of cases reported in 2024. As current pertussis diagnostics are predominantly based on molecular methods, cultured isolates are increasingly scarce, limiting traditional culture-based surveillance. To address these challenges, this study evaluated culture-independent approaches for B. pertussis surveillance and their feasibility for implementation in public health laboratory settings in Victoria, Australia. The Microbiological Diagnostic Unit Public Health Laboratory received 356 nasopharyngeal clinical specimens that were PCR-positive for Bordetella spp. from diagnostic laboratories for further characterisation during the 2024-2025 epidemic period. Culture-based approaches yielded only five B. pertussis isolates, largely due to limitations associated with specimen transport media. Four culture-independent approaches were evaluated for B. pertussis characterisation: real-time PCR assay for high-resolution Bordetella spp. differentiation (n=356), multiplex PCR amplicon sequencing assay for lineage typing (n=38), in-house laboratory developed test implemented on Panther Fusion(R) System for macrolide resistance screening (n=92) and shotgun metagenomic sequencing (n=5). The dataset was dominated by B. pertussis (330/356; 92.7%) with most strains harbouring ptxP3 (35/38; 92.1%) allele and the macrolide resistance rate was reported as 4.3% (4/92). Shotgun metagenomics was able to detect B. pertussis directly from clinical samples, but the genomic recovery was limited. Evaluation of operational performance and workflow integration highlighted method-specific strengths and limitations, informing suitability for implementation in public health laboratories. This study demonstrates the potential to integrate culture-independent approaches into public health laboratory settings to strengthen B. pertussis surveillance and inform feasible workflow design amid limited culture availability.

papers.title: IVA, a locally deployable Intelligent Variant Analyser based on a small language model for complete case-level and trio-based genomic interpretation.
papers.abstract: Background: Recent work has brought large language models (LLMs) into clinical variant interpretation. In most existing approaches, the model is confined to text-level operations, retrieving, extracting, compacting, and summarizing heterogeneous evidence, while the genuine genetic evaluation is delegated to a separate deterministic engine. Other tools employ LLMs to mine functional evidence for a single ACMG criterion, to rerank a classifier's output, or to answer isolated variant questions. Integrative genetic reasoning, by contrast, demands multi-source evidence weighing for each variant, reconciliation of inheritance with observed zygosity and parental genotypes, joint interpretation of variants in the same gene, and the derivation of a case-level conclusion. Moreover, to protect patient privacy, this must be done on hospital premises. Methods: o build an end-to-end variant interpreter that runs on local infrastructure, we benchmarked 13 small language models (SLMs) on 150 multiple-choice genetics questions and selected Qwen3.5-9B. In IVA (Intelligent Variant Analyser), a four-stage pipeline, the model assigns ACMG/AMP criteria, applies de novo, dominant, recessive, and X-linked inheritance logic to trios, and writes a structured report, while deterministic code handles retrieval, phasing, point summation, citation checking, and formatting. We evaluated IVA on synthetic scenarios, 16 solved trios, and 327 solved singleton cases of visual impairment, on a single GPU. Results: On the benchmark, Qwen3.5-9B reached a mean accuracy of 0.81, compared with 0.89 for a 1.6-trillion-parameter cloud model. In the 16 trios, IVA reported every previously identified pathogenic, likely pathogenic, or uncertain-significance variant of interest (sensitivity 100%; precision 39.5%). In the 327 singleton cases, it recovered 93% of the expert-reported causative variants and classified 82% of them as pathogenic or likely pathogenic (precision 43%). Failures fell into four recurrent classes: omission, unverified mechanism, mismatch between reasoning and label, and arithmetic errors. Conclusions: A small language model running on local hardware can serve as the reasoning layer for case-level and trio-based variant interpretation when it is surrounded by deterministic safeguards. Because its outputs are not deterministic, analyst review and prospective multicenter validation remain necessary.

papers.title: AI-assisted identification of potential treatment injury from inpatient discharge summaries: an early-stage sociotechnical evaluation in a New Zealand district hospital
papers.abstract: Objectives: To assess the feasibility and early performance of an AI-assisted screening workflow that reviews inpatient discharge summaries to identify potential treatment injuries for clinician review and, where appropriate, Accident Compensation Corporation (ACC) treatment injury claim consideration in New Zealand. Design: Single-site, six-month pilot reported as a quality-improvement/service-evaluation activity. A large language model (LLM)-enabled system acted as an index screening test over discharge summaries to generate candidate treatment injury signals for structured clinician adjudication and escalation. Setting: A New Zealand district hospital (Wairarapa). Screening operated on routinely produced inpatient discharge summaries. Participants: All inpatient discharge summaries produced during the pilot period were screened (n = 2,642). The unit of analysis was one discharge summary per inpatient episode. Intervention: An LLM-based screening workflow that outputs structured candidate harm signals with supporting excerpts and a certainty label. Outputs were reviewed by clinicians using a structured adjudication template. Suitable cases could be escalated to senior clinicians and followed through the local ACC treatment injury process. Main outcome measures: Primary outcomes were yield, positive predictive value (PPV) of AI- flagged signals for clinician-adjudicated iatrogenic harm, and the rate of unsupported/hallucinated outputs. Secondary outcomes included overlap with incident reporting and administrative coding, downstream ACC claim outcomes, and clinician review workload. Results: Across 2,642 inpatient discharge summaries screened, the AI-assisted workflow generated 237 candidate signals (yield 9.0%; 95% CI 7.9% to 10.1%). Clinician adjudication classified 102 as confirmed iatrogenic harm, 43 as possible harm requiring additional context, 81 as no harm, and 11 as unsupported/hallucinated outputs. PPV for confirmed harm was 43.0% (95% CI 36.8% to 49.4%). PPV for confirmed-or-possible harm was 61.2% (95% CI 54.9% to 67.1%). Seven ACC treatment injury claims were lodged as a direct result of AI-assisted surfacing; three were accepted, two declined, and two were held/pending at analysis. Organisational ACC data identified 68 treatment injury claims lodged during the same period, of which 17 overlapped with AI-identified cases. Conclusions: AI-assisted screening of discharge summaries can feasibly increase detection of potential treatment injuries for structured clinician review and may support more systematic ACC consideration and safety learning. Safe scaling requires transparent reporting of model and prompt details, robust human adjudication and escalation pathways, and governance controls to mitigate false positives and unsupported outputs. A next-stage evaluation should estimate diagnostic accuracy against a chart-review reference standard and examine implementation outcomes including workload, acceptability, fidelity and sustainability.

papers.title: Effects of Dish Name, Visible Amount, Persona, and Explicit Instruction on Energy Estimates From Food Photographs by 26 Vision-Language Models: Comparative Evaluation Study
papers.abstract: Background: Vision-language models (VLMs) are being considered for estimating energy intake from meal photographs. Prompt descriptions such as a Japanese-dietitian persona shift the estimates, suggesting their use for calibration; what the estimates rest on was unknown. Objective: We examined whether prompt descriptions can serve as calibration, at which training stage responses to a nationality persona and to an amount instruction arise, and whether estimates follow the visible amount or one associated with the identified dish. Methods: Eleven commercial and 15 open-weight models were evaluated on NutriImage (887 Japanese single-dish photographs) and SNAPMe (1,134 US meal photographs) under eight prompt conditions (no description, five personas, and smaller- or larger-portion instructions). With one model, images were cropped or replaced by the dish name. Before- and after-meal photographs of 804 meals (ACETADA) were estimated. Pre-trained and post-trained weights of Gemma 3 and InternVL3.5 8B were compared by likelihood scoring. Prompts were compared with numerical calibration. Results: Where the dish was named as in the full image, a 25% crop changed neither the median absolute percentage error (MedAPE; 33.8% vs 34.4%) nor the persona shift (-20 vs -20 kcal); dish names alone gave similar accuracy (MedAPE 31.7%); nearly empty trays still received 39%-75% of the before-meal estimate, often described as already eaten. Between models, the persona shift was related to baseline bias (r = -0.77) and less to instruction following (r = -0.36); the instruction shift showed the reverse (r = -0.14 and -0.95). In Gemma 3, the Japan-US contrast was 2-4 times larger before post-training, and the instruction response 2-4 times larger after it (InternVL3.5 8B: 3 and 1.4 times). Across images, the Japan-US contrast was uniform on US meals and, for Japanese dishes in the commercial models, Gemma 3, and Qwen3-VL 32B, larger where overestimated. In these models, the persona lowered MedAPE for Japanese dishes as much as, or slightly more than, subtracting the mean bias, and no more than dividing by a ratio; on US meals it did not; in open-weight families that responded little, only numerical calibration lowered error. The smaller-portion instruction raised MedAPE in models with little bias (eg, 30.0% to 50.2%). Conclusions: In the model examined most closely, the estimates behaved as if anchored on an amount associated with the identified dish and only partly corrected by the visible amount. Prompt descriptions moved them by amounts depending on model and cuisine, not on the correction needed; a persona is therefore not proposed as a general means of calibration. In a facility, the findings suggest showing the identified dish for correction, calibrating by a ratio measured on reference meals with the deployed model, keeping amount statements out of the prompt, and not deriving intake from before-after-meal differences.

papers.title: MedMatch: a standardized medication order format for data science and natural language processing applications
papers.abstract: Background: Without automation, evaluation of medication management with large language models (LLMs) is largely limited to resource-intensive clinician evaluation. The purpose of this study was to develop a standardized medication structure (MedMatch) that supports automated evaluation. Methods: Our goal was to create a medication order format with face validity to a clinician panel that maximizes clarity and safety. We used a multi-step process including (1) clinician survey of medication orders, (2) clinician survey of order appropriateness, (3) order sentence structure formation, (4) benchmark experiment development, and (5) GPT-5-chat testing across multiple experiments, which included assessment of ability to transform a medication order into MedMatch format and identify the route of an order sentence and ability to identify missing order components. Results: First, lexical overlap analysis demonstrated pattern norms with specific components appearing most commonly in order of drug name, dose, unit, route, and frequency. Secondly, formal written orders consistently showed low omissions and high overlap and were deemed more appropriate as computer-generated orders. Third, MedMatch formats were created for oral and intravenous routes. Fourth, benchmark datasets and an abbreviation document were created. Fifth, GPT-5-Chat accuracy on MedMatch order standardization was highest in intravenous push (96.7%), oral liquid (86.1%), and intravenous intermittent (85%) categories. Overall performance was 77.6%. Identification of missing order components was improved with the MedMatch format (76.8% vs. 66.7%). Conclusions: This is the first attempt to create and assess standardized medication order formatting to support benchmarking performance of LLMs. Limitations identified here demonstrate the need for medication-specific methodology.

papers.title: RadKev: An Open-Weight Decision Model for Radiology
papers.abstract: Background: Many radiology decisions, such as whether a report describes a finding or how urgently a study should be read, are choices among a fixed set of answers. Decision models return a probability for each permitted answer in one step, without generating text, and an open-weight model can run within a hospital so that patient data stay local. No decision model has yet been specialized for radiology and compared with large language models (LLMs). Methods: We fine-tuned the general-purpose decision models Kev-27B (Qwen3.8-27B backbone) and Kev-9B on 36,109 records from public radiology datasets to obtain RadKev-27B and RadKev-9B, and compared them with the Kev models, the hosted decision models Jev and OpenAI Decisions, and the LLM Qwen3.8-27B, on 14,142 held-out questions in fifteen tasks (report reading, case diagnosis and classification, radiological knowledge). The prespecified primary outcome was task-averaged accuracy relative to Kev-27B. Results: RadKev-27B exceeded Kev-27B by 4.9 percentage points (95% CI 3.8 to 6.2), with the largest gain in report error detection (22.6 points); RadKev-9B exceeded Kev-9B by 6.9 points (5.5 to 8.4) and did not differ detectably from Kev-27B, a model three times its size. RadKev-27B was more accurate than the hosted decision models Jev (3.0 points, 1.7 to 4.4) and OpenAI Decisions (4.8, 3.2 to 6.4), than Qwen3.8-27B without reasoning (4.7, 3.4 to 6.0) and with reasoning (2.8 points, 1.0 to 4.6) on 1,675 questions, at 132-fold lower latency (128 ms vs 16.9 s per question). At an error rate of 5%, RadKev-27B could answer 90.5% of questions and Kev-27B 76.4%. Conclusions: RadKev-27B was more accurate than two hosted decision models and an LLM of the same size, with or without reasoning, at a fraction of the latency of reasoning, and can be deployed within an institution for categorical radiology decisions after validation on local data.

papers.title: Multimodal Machine Learning-Based Clinical and Genomic Prognostic Factors for Progression-Free Survival in Metastatic Breast Cancer Using Phase III MONALEESA Trials
papers.abstract: Purpose: Cyclin-dependent kinase 4/6 inhibitors in combination with endocrine therapy have become widely adopted as a first-line treatment approach for hormone receptor-positive (HR+)/human epidermal growth factor receptor 2-negative (HER2-) advanced breast cancer (ABC). Through a collaboration between Novartis and the US Food and Drug Administration, we integrated multimodal data from phase III MONALEESA trials to identify novel prognostic factors for HR+/HER2- ABC. Experimental Design: Baseline clinical and genomics data were collected from patients in the MONALEESA-2, -3, and -7 trials. Circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) from plasma samples and gene expression in archival tumor biopsies were analyzed. Machine learning models were trained (n = 1,355) on progression-free survival (PFS) using multimodal features via fusion models. In a test set (n = 382), prognostic performances were evaluated using the Kaplan-Meier, Cox, and Weibull models. Results: The late fusion model achieved a prognostic performance (C-index: 0.727, 95% CI: 0.641-0.799) slightly outperforming early fusion (C-index: 0.718, 95% CI: 0.631-0.791) and single-modality models. Model-based risk stratification identified distinct low- and high-risk groups (PFS HR, 0.28; 95% CI: 0.20-0.38). Among the top 40 features for progression risk (18 clinical, 20 gene expression, and 2 ctDNA), these were associated with higher risk: liver involvement, higher histological grades, early relapse; lower STC2 and RBBP8 expressions and higher FBX05 expression; and higher tumor mutational burden and ctDNA purity. Conclusions: Integrating clinical and genomic modalities improved progression risk prediction compared with single-modality models, while highlighting salient features that inform the underlying biology and support hypothesis generation.

papers.title: Posttraumatic Stress Disorder Epigenome-Wide Association Studies in the Million Veteran Program
papers.abstract: Genomic studies have improved our understanding of posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) biology. Epigenetic differences in DNA methylation can reflect environmental influences, which are critical in PTSD etiology, and may additionally differentiate between PTSD cases and controls or distinguish severity of PTSD symptoms. We conducted epigenome-wide association studies (EWAS) of PTSD in 22,141 subjects from the United States V.A. Million Veteran Program (MVP), using the PTSD Checklist (PCL-C), including 17,674 European ancestry (EUR), 3,430 African ancestry (AFR), and 1,037 admixed American descent (AMR) individuals. We evaluated the 17-item PCL-C and its symptom subdomains (re-experiencing, avoidance, and hyperarousal) and used our previously-reported algorithmically-defined PTSD diagnoses validated against clinical records. There were 9,413 total cases of Lifetime PTSD and 27,257 controls, with 5,184 cases and 19,382 controls in EUR, 3,095 cases and 6,240 controls in AFR, and 1,134 cases and 1,635 controls in AMR. We identified a total of 272 epigenome-wide-significant associated CpG sites across all PTSD traits, or 28 after adjusting for smoking status. We replicated 5 out of 11 CpG sites reported in a prior (Psychiatric Genomics Consortium) PTSD EWAS. There was significant enrichment of genes downregulated in somatostatin interneurons and of genes expressed in GABAergic interneurons. Regression analyses showed that PTSD case status was significantly correlated with accelerated DNA methylation aging. Contrary to previous PTSD EWAS findings, smoking status stratification suggested that the association between PTSD and methylation of the AHRR gene may be confounded by smoking status. This is the largest-scale PTSD EWAS in multiple ancestries and the first large PTSD EWAS on symptom severity. We replicate findings from previous EWAS and greatly extend knowledge of the epigenetics of PTSD.

papers.title: Measuring enteric pathogen force of infection through antibody responses in children
papers.abstract: Enteric pathogens account for a substantial global disease burden, yet population-based surveillance remains limited by the transient nature of pathogen shedding, which constrains the sensitivity of stool-based molecular testing to a narrow detection window. Detection of IgG responses in serological surveys could enable new insights into enteric pathogen transmission, but benchmarking serological measures relative to stool-based measures of infection remains a critical evidence gap. We compared measures of disease transmission in longitudinal birth cohort samples using multiplex IgG (1,601 dried blood spots, 370 children) and PCR assays (2,231 stool samples, 370 children) that overlapped for nine pathogens (norovirus GI, GII, Shigella/enteroinvasive Escherichia coli (EIEC), Campylobacter spp., enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli (LT-ETEC), Salmonella enterica, Giardia spp., Cryptosporidium spp., Entamoeba histolytica). LT-ETEC and Campylobacter ranked highest while E. histolytica and S. enterica ranked lowest by both IgG and PCR measures of infection. Measures of infection were less aligned for norovirus GI, norovirus GII, Cryptosporidium, Shigella/EIEC, and Giardia. Despite this, for most pathogens, and across both measures, force of infection was lowest in the urban city of Esmeraldas and substantially higher in more rural populations, with relative risks in assay measures (seroconversion rate and PCR detected prevalence) over 2.0 for pathogens with the largest differences (Shigella/EIEC and norovirus GI). Together, our results suggest that although absolute levels of infection differed between assays, IgG and PCR captured consistent relative risk of infection across geographic strata, suggesting either method can identify high- versus low-transmission settings.

papers.title: Feasibility and Measurement Properties of a Large Language Model-Based Virtual Patient Laboratory for Clinical Reasoning Training in Physical Therapy Students: Single-Arm Pilot Study
papers.abstract: Background: Large language models (LLMs) configured as virtual patients may expand structured practice of clinical reasoning in health professions education. Before testing effectiveness, it must be established whether students engage with them and whether the resulting scores are complete, reliable, and related to performance with real patients. Our earlier pilot randomized trial found very low engagement with a less structured LLM-based approach. Objective: This study aimed to assess the feasibility (adherence, acceptability, and data completeness) of a revised, structured LLM-based clinical reasoning laboratory (Laboratorio de Inteligencia Artificial [LIA]) in undergraduate physical therapy education and to explore its measurement properties, including its association with clinical judgment with a real patient assessed with the Lasater Clinical Judgment Rubric (LCJR). Methods: In this single-arm pilot feasibility study, 27 third-year physical therapy students at a Spanish university completed, in 2024-2025, 3 virtual patient cases (lumbar, cervical, and thoracic spine pain) simulated by ChatGPT (GPT-4) over 4 weeks, each twice. ChatGPT scored each attempt from 0 to 4 on the same 10 dimensions of the Lasater Clinical Judgment Rubric (LCJR; 0-40 points) that human assessors applied (1-4 per dimension; 10-40 points) during a real patient encounter. Feasibility outcomes were case completion, data completeness, and satisfaction (0-10). Measurement outcomes were internal consistency and convergent validity (Spearman correlations between model-generated and human LCJR scores). Variability estimates informed the sample size of a future trial. Results: All 27 students were assessed with the LCJR; 22 (81%) completed at least 1 LIA case. Both attempts of the lumbar, cervical, and thoracic cases were completed by 78%, 63%, and 74% of students, respectively. Satisfaction data were available for 15 students (56%; mean 6.0, SD 1.3), and missing secondary data clustered in the third rotation. Internal consistency was excellent for the LCJR (alpha=.96) and ranged from .43 to .90 for model-generated ratings. Model-generated LIA scores clustered near the maximum (mean 36.0, SD 1.4). Among completers, LIA scores correlated weakly with the LCJR (rho=0.25, 95% CI -0.20 to 0.61; rho=0.44, 95% CI 0.05-0.71, when noncompleted attempts were scored as 0). Grade point average correlated almost perfectly with the LCJR (rho=0.96; n=22); after adjustment for it, the LIA-LCJR association disappeared (partial rho=-0.10). A future trial would require approximately 39 students per group (80% power, conservative variance). Conclusions: Delivering the LIA within the curriculum was feasible, but clinical judgment ratings generated by ChatGPT did not reflect those of human assessors with a real patient: they clustered near the maximum and showed no convergent validity once noncompletion was separated from performance. LLM-generated ratings should not be used as outcome or assessment measures without validation against human raters. Case calibration, completion tracking, and clarification of the GPA-LCJR relationship are also needed before a definitive trial. Trial Registration: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT06809634; https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06809634

papers.title: Benchmark Self-Triage (BeST): Comparing Self-Triage Systems and Multiple Generations of OpenAI Models Against Preliminary Expert Consensus
papers.abstract: As digital self-triage becomes more widely used, quality assurance requires evaluation of both emergency recognition and overall agreement with clinical judgement, including how these outcomes differ across generations of large language models. The Benchmark Self-Triage (BeST) project intends to provide a framework to compare systems for digital self-triage against a medical 'gold standard' in Germany. In a first step developing the method and demonstrating its potential we developed a representative set of patient vignettes and compared two regulated medical-device triage systems, SmED and Infermedica, with five structured OpenAI configurations spanning multiple model generations: gpt-4.1, gpt-5.4, gpt-5.6-luna, gpt-5.6-sol, and gpt-6-astra. An LLM-based patient actor covered 480 physician-curated vignettes derived from German routine triage data. A pool of seven physicians provided preliminary reference classifications and consensus for 480 vignettes. Recommendations were mapped to three urgency categories 'emergency', 'acute', and 'not urgent' and evaluated using winsorised weights derived from routine triage frequencies. Weighted emergency sensitivity ranged from 51.3% (95% CI 35.5-66.3%) for gpt-4.1 to 99.9% (99.7-100.0%) for gpt-6-astra. Weighted exact three-category agreement (accuracy) ranged from 54.4% to 68.8%; gpt-4.1 achieved the highest agreement despite the lowest emergency sensitivity. No system performed best across all urgency categories. The later-generation OpenAI configurations showed a more precautionary triage profile resembling SmED, with higher sensitivity for emergency cases; gpt-6-astra showed the strongest shift. This cross-sectional comparison across model generations suggests a shift towards more precautionary triage behaviour, without establishing a longitudinal improvement in accuracy. These findings highlight the limitations of overall agreement for evaluating self-triage and support category-specific assessment. Broader expert consensus and evaluation, as well as further steps to reduce dependence on SmED-derived source data, are needed and planned before drawing conclusions about clinical safety.

papers.title: Quantifying Cancer Clinical Trial Eligibility Using Artificial Intelligence-Based Matching
papers.abstract: PURPOSE: To develop and validate an artificial intelligence-enabled platform that combines efficient screening with explicit eligibility logic by converting unstructured cancer trial criteria into reusable structured queries, and illustrates potential eligibility using synthetic patients. METHODS: We downloaded actively recruiting US interventional treatment trials for advanced/metastatic breast cancer, colon cancer, and non-small cell lung cancer from ClinicalTrials.gov. Medical oncologists created 24 synthetic patient vignettes. A large language model converted trial eligibility criteria into Structured Query Language (SQL) code and patient information into structured records, enabling rule-based matching without further LLM inference. Cancer details and treatment history were considered, but not laboratory results or comorbidities. Validation included physician editing of generated eligibility code for 30 trials and independent assessments by two physicians, followed by consensus adjudication, for eligibility across ten trials. We descriptively summarized potential eligibility by trial characteristics and when varying age, ECOG performance status, sex, and ZIP code. RESULTS: Of 833 candidate trials, 746 met inclusion criteria. Performing matching for all 746 trials took a median of 0.459 seconds per patient, excluding patient-data preparation. Against physician consensus, automated matching agreed on 230/240 patient-trial pairs (95.8%; sensitivity 83.3%, specificity 100%). Across synthetic patients, potentially eligible trials ranged from 10 to 258 without geographic restrictions. Counts decreased with worse performance status and geographic restriction and were relatively stable across ages 30-90. Later-phase, randomized, and molecularly selective trials generally matched fewer vignettes. CONCLUSION: LLM-generated SQL enables rapid, explicit rule-based screening for potential trial eligibility. Evaluation in synthetic vignettes supports feasibility, while missed matches underscore the need for further validation.
